What a naive before/after eval comparison misses is usually the same thing: average-case quality on a broad benchmark can look nearly identical between teacher and student while the student has quietly degraded disproportionately on rare, high-stakes edge cases -- the exact clauses, exceptions, and unusual document structures that a document review pipeline exists to catch in the first place, precisely because those rare cases are underrepresented in whatever distillation dataset was used to train the student. A serious evaluation specifically stratifies by rarity and stakes, not just aggregate accuracy, and compares student-versus-teacher agreement specifically on the hardest, highest-stakes slice of the distribution, not just the easy bulk of it.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd explain distillation first: you're training a smaller student model to mimic a larger teacher's behavior, usually using the teacher's own outputs as training targets, so the student learns to approximate the teacher's decision boundary rather than learning the task from raw labels alone. Done well, you recover a good chunk of the teacher's quality at a fraction of the cost and latency, because the student's smaller by construction.

But I'd push the team to check two simpler alternatives first, because distillation has real upfront engineering cost -- generating teacher outputs across a representative dataset, training the student, validating it carefully. Better prompting against the existing model is worth ruling out first, even though it doesn't cut serving cost. And a smaller model fine-tuned directly on labeled task data, skipping the teacher-output-generation step entirely, is often nearly as good for well-defined tasks. Distillation earns its complexity specifically when the task involves nuanced judgment calls that are easier to demonstrate through the teacher's outputs than to write as clean labels -- and document review, which is full of exactly that kind of judgment call, is actually a reasonable case for it.

The thing I'd insist on before calling this done is the eval methodology, not just a top-line before/after number. Aggregate accuracy can look nearly identical between teacher and student while the student has quietly gotten worse specifically on the rare, high-stakes edge cases -- the unusual clause, the exception buried in page forty -- precisely because those cases are underrepresented in the distillation data. I'd stratify the eval by rarity and stakes and specifically check student-versus-teacher agreement on the hardest slice, not just the easy bulk, before trusting this is actually ready.
questions.example: A realistic pattern: aggregate accuracy on a 500-document eval set shows the distilled student at 94% versus the teacher's 96% -- a small, apparently acceptable gap -- but on the 30 documents in that set flagged as containing an unusual indemnification clause specifically, the student's accuracy drops to 71% versus the teacher's 93%, a gap the aggregate number completely hid.
commonMistakes: Treating distillation as always strictly better than simpler alternatives like prompting or direct fine-tuning on labels
Not checking whether request volume justifies the upfront engineering cost of building a distillation pipeline
Assuming distillation transfers the teacher's full general reasoning rather than competence on the specific distilled distribution
Evaluating only aggregate accuracy and missing disproportionate degradation on rare, high-stakes edge cases
Treating a successful aggregate before/after comparison as sufficient validation for a high-stakes task like document review
keyPoints: Distillation trains a smaller student to approximate a teacher's decision boundary, usually via the teacher's own outputs
It's worth the investment only at sufficient volume, with a narrow enough task, and a quality bar that tolerates a gap to the teacher
Simpler alternatives (better prompting, direct fine-tuning on labels) should be ruled out first
Distillation doesn't transfer general reasoning, only competence on the distribution it was distilled against
Aggregate before/after comparisons can hide disproportionate degradation on rare, high-stakes edge cases

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the distillation mechanism
Correctly identifies the volume/task conditions that justify distillation over simpler alternatives
Correctly identifies simpler alternatives worth ruling out first
Identifies the stratified-eval blind spot a naive comparison misses
Clarity

questions.title: Designing an Org-Wide Eval-Regression CI Gate Across Dozens of Services
questions.prompt: Marlowe Capital has forty-plus services calling into shared model endpoints, each with its own ad-hoc eval script, and no org-wide way to block a model or prompt-template change that regresses quality anywhere downstream. Design and sketch the skeleton of an org-wide eval-regression CI gate: what it checks, where it sits in the deploy pipeline, and how it scales to many services without becoming a bottleneck that teams route around.
questions.modelAnswer:
The gate has three jobs: run each service's eval suite against the candidate model or prompt-template version, compare the result against that service's own stored baseline with actual significance testing (not a raw delta), and block the deploy specifically for that service if the drop exceeds a threshold the service owner, not the platform team, has set in advance. It sits as a required check in the deploy pipeline immediately before any model/prompt-template version change reaches production traffic, the same position a test suite occupies in normal CI, and critically it runs per-service against that service's own eval suite and baseline, not a single shared platform-wide eval, because what counts as a regression for claims summarization is a different question than what counts as one for a compliance search tool.

The skeleton above shows the key design decision: a declarative per-service config (eval suite location, baseline model reference, regression threshold, and whether a failure actually blocks the deploy or just alerts) that the service owner registers once with the platform, rather than the platform team hardcoding logic per service. The gate runner itself is generic -- load baseline scores, run the suite against the candidate, run a significance test respecting the service's own minimum sample size, and either block or alert based on that service's own configured policy. This is what lets it scale to forty-plus services without becoming a bottleneck: the platform team maintains one gate runner, not forty bespoke scripts, and each service team owns their own eval suite content and threshold without needing the platform team in the loop for every tuning change.

The part that actually prevents teams from routing around the gate is making the blocking behavior opt-in but strongly incentivized, with a visible exception process rather than a silent bypass: a service can mark itself non-blocking (alert only) during a documented ramp-up period, but that status is visible in a shared dashboard so platform leadership can see which services haven't yet adopted a hard gate, which turns 'routing around it' into a tracked, visible decision rather than an invisible one.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd frame the gate's three jobs clearly: run each service's own eval suite against the candidate version, compare it to that service's own baseline with real significance testing instead of eyeballing a raw score delta, and block the deploy if it crosses a threshold the service owner set themselves, not one the platform team imposed.

The architecture decision that actually lets this scale to forty-plus services is the declarative config -- each team registers their eval suite location, baseline reference, and threshold once, and the gate runner itself stays generic and platform-owned, so we're maintaining one runner, not forty bespoke CI scripts. And I'd make blocking opt-in during a ramp-up window but visible on a shared dashboard, because the moment a non-blocking exception becomes invisible, teams quietly stay in alert-only mode forever and the gate stops meaning anything.
commonMistakes: Building one shared platform-wide eval suite instead of letting each service own its own eval content and threshold
Comparing candidate scores to baseline with a raw delta instead of a significance test with a minimum sample size
Hardcoding per-service logic into the gate runner instead of a declarative config each team registers
Allowing silent, invisible bypass of the blocking gate instead of a tracked, visible exception process
keyPoints: The gate runs per-service against that service's own eval suite and self-set threshold, not one shared platform eval
Comparison uses significance testing with a minimum sample size, not a raw score delta
A declarative per-service config plus one generic, platform-owned gate runner is what makes it scale
Blocking status is visible on a shared dashboard so bypass is a tracked decision, not a silent one

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Designs a gate that checks significance-tested regression per service, not a raw delta
Correctly separates the generic gate runner from per-service declarative configuration
Places the gate correctly in the deploy pipeline as a blocking pre-production check
Addresses how the design prevents teams from quietly bypassing the gate
Code/skeleton clarity

questions.title: Writing a Kill-Switch Mechanism for an Agent Platform
questions.prompt: Clearwater Mutual's agent platform runs dozens of autonomous agents across customer service, claims, and internal tooling. Leadership wants a company-wide kill switch that can halt any agent, a class of agents, or the entire platform within seconds during an incident, without requiring a code deploy. Write the skeleton of this kill-switch mechanism and explain the design decisions that make it fast and trustworthy during an actual incident.
questions.modelAnswer:
The design has to satisfy two requirements that pull against each other: it has to propagate near-instantly (seconds, as leadership requires), and it has to be checked cheaply enough on every single agent step that adding the check doesn't itself become a latency or cost problem across dozens of agents running constantly. The skeleton resolves this with a tiered check: the kill-switch state lives in a fast, highly-available shared store (not a config file requiring a deploy, and not a database requiring a slow query), and each orchestrator instance keeps a very short-TTL local cache of that state so the hot path of every agent step is a cheap in-memory check almost all of the time, falling back to the shared store only when the local cache has expired -- a 2-second TTL means a trip propagates to every running agent instance within roughly that window without every single step paying a network round-trip.

The scope hierarchy (global, class, individual agent) is checked at every step specifically so an incident responder isn't forced to choose between 'halt everything' and 'halt nothing' -- a prompt-injection incident traced to one specific agent can be contained by tripping just that agent's switch, while a platform-wide model-provider issue can be contained with the global switch, without those two response shapes requiring different mechanisms. Checking at every step, not just session start, matters because a long-running agent mid-task needs to actually stop mid-task when tripped, not finish its current multi-step run first -- an incident responder tripping the switch and then watching agents keep running for another twenty steps because the check only happened at the start is a design that fails exactly when it's needed most.

The trustworthiness piece is the audit log and the asymmetric approval requirement: tripping the switch is a single action, deliberately low-friction, because during an incident you want zero friction to stop something dangerous; resetting it requires a second approver by default, because the cost of accidentally leaving something halted a little longer is low, while the cost of prematurely un-halting something that's still actively causing harm is high, and that asymmetry should be reflected directly in the approval friction on each action.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The tension I'd design around is speed versus cost -- this needs to propagate in seconds, but it also gets checked on every single step of every agent running on the platform, so the check itself can't be slow or expensive. I'd put the actual state in a fast, shared store, not a config file that needs a deploy, and give each orchestrator a very short local cache -- a couple of seconds -- so almost every step check is just an in-memory read, and a trip still reaches every running instance within that short window.

The scope hierarchy matters a lot here -- global, agent-class, and individual-agent -- because an incident responder needs to be able to halt exactly the blast radius of the actual problem. If it's one misbehaving agent, I don't want the only available response to be 'take down the whole platform.' And I'd check this at every step, not just at session start, because a long-running agent needs to actually stop mid-task, not finish its current run first -- that's the failure mode that makes a kill switch useless exactly when you need it.

For trust, I'd make tripping it a single, low-friction action -- during an incident, you want zero friction to stop something dangerous -- but require a second approver to reset it, because leaving something halted a little too long is a much smaller cost than un-halting something that's still actively causing harm. And every trip and reset gets written to an audit log with who and why, because this is exactly the kind of control a post-incident review and a compliance audit will both want a clean record of.
questions.example: A real scenario: a prompt-injection attack is traced specifically to the claims-adjuster-v3 agent class at 2:14am; the on-call engineer trips the scope 'class:claims-adjuster' from a dashboard with no code deploy, and every running instance of that agent class halts mid-step within roughly 2 seconds, while every other agent class on the platform keeps running unaffected.
commonMistakes: Checking the kill switch only at session start instead of at every agent step
Storing kill-switch state in a config file or database requiring a deploy or slow query to change
Having only a single global on/off switch with no scoped granularity for agent class or individual agent
Making both trip and reset equally low-friction, ignoring the real asymmetry in the cost of each mistake
Not writing an audit log entry for every trip and reset action
keyPoints: State lives in a fast, highly-available store with a short local cache, not a config file requiring a deploy
The check runs at every agent step, not just session start, so a halted agent actually stops mid-task
A scope hierarchy (global/class/agent) lets responders halt exactly the blast radius of the actual problem
Tripping is low-friction by design; resetting requires a second approver, reflecting the real cost asymmetry
Every trip and reset is written to an audit log for incident review and compliance

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Designs fast state propagation without making per-step checks expensive
Implements a correct scope hierarchy for contained blast-radius response
Checks at every step, not just session start
Designs the correct trip/reset friction asymmetry with audit logging
Code clarity

questions.title: Writing a Tenant-Isolation Enforcement Layer for a Shared Vector Store
questions.prompt: Kingsmere Retail serves dozens of enterprise customers from one shared vector database for its RAG platform, and a recent near-miss showed that a misconfigured retrieval query could have returned one tenant's documents to another tenant's chat session. Write the skeleton of a tenant-isolation enforcement layer that makes this structurally impossible rather than relying on every query being written correctly, and explain the design principle behind it.
questions.modelAnswer:
The near-miss happened because tenant filtering was almost certainly implemented as a parameter some caller was responsible for passing correctly on each query, which means every single call site across the codebase is a place the isolation guarantee could be forgotten, misconfigured, or bypassed, and at enterprise scale with many engineers touching the retrieval code over time, that's not a hypothetical, it's a matter of when, not if. The fix is a structural one: tenant scoping can't be a parameter the caller remembers to pass, it has to be a property bound once, at construction, into an object that makes it physically impossible to query without that scope applied -- the skeleton above does this by never exposing a method that accepts tenant_id from the caller at query time at all; the only way to get a working retriever instance is to construct it with a tenant_id resolved from authentication, and every query that instance makes is automatically filtered to that tenant with no code path that skips it.

The second structural piece is defense in depth beyond the query filter itself: even with a correct filter clause, I'd never trust the filter alone to be the only thing standing between a bug and cross-tenant leakage, because a vector database's filter implementation, an index corruption, or a future migration bug could still return a mismatched result. The post-query verification step -- checking every returned result's actual stored tenant_id against the expected tenant before returning it to the caller -- is what catches that class of failure even when the filter itself somehow failed, and it logs a security event specifically when it catches something, which turns a near-miss like the one described into a loud, actionable alert instead of a silent pass.

The design principle underneath both of these: isolation has to be enforced by the architecture in a way that makes the correct behavior the only possible behavior, not by code review catching every query that's written correctly. A security control that depends on every engineer remembering to do something right, forever, across every future change, is not actually a control -- it's a hope.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The real problem with the near-miss isn't that one query was written wrong, it's that the architecture made it possible for a query to be written wrong at all -- if tenant filtering is a parameter every caller has to remember to pass correctly, that's a guarantee that depends on every engineer getting it right forever, which isn't actually a guarantee.

So the fix I'd ship is structural: tenant scope gets bound once, at construction, into a retriever object, and there's no method on it that even accepts a tenant_id from the caller at query time -- the only way to get a working instance is through an authenticated request handler that resolves the real tenant and constructs the retriever with it baked in. That removes the entire class of 'someone forgot to pass the filter' bugs, because there's no code path where that's even possible.

And I wouldn't stop at the filter -- I'd add a post-query verification step that checks every returned result's actual stored tenant against what we expect, even though the filter should have already guaranteed that, because a filter implementation bug, an index issue, or a future migration mistake could still slip something through, and I want that caught and logged loudly as a security event, not silently passed along. The underlying principle is: don't build a control that depends on every future query being written correctly -- build one where the incorrect behavior is structurally impossible to reach.
questions.example: The near-miss itself: a query omitted the tenant filter clause due to a copy-pasted code path from a different, tenant-agnostic internal tool; with the TenantScopedRetriever design, that exact copy-paste mistake can't happen because there's no constructor or method signature that allows building a retriever without a tenant_id, and no query method that accepts an override.
commonMistakes: Implementing tenant scoping as a parameter callers pass per-query instead of binding it once at construction
Trusting the vector database's filter clause as the sole mechanism without a post-query verification step
Allowing a caller-supplied extra filter to override the bound tenant_id
Not logging a security event when a post-query verification check catches a mismatch
Relying on code review to catch every future query instead of making the incorrect behavior structurally impossible
keyPoints: Tenant scope is bound once at construction, never passed as a per-query caller parameter
No code path exists that allows querying without the bound tenant filter applied
Post-query verification of each result's actual tenant provides defense in depth beyond the filter itself
Security events are logged when verification catches a mismatch, turning near-misses into actionable alerts
The core principle is making incorrect behavior structurally impossible, not relying on every query being written correctly

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Designs tenant binding at construction time, not as a per-call parameter
Includes post-query verification as defense in depth
Prevents callers from overriding the bound tenant scope
Articulates the structural-impossibility design principle clearly
Code clarity

questions.title: Implementing a Cost-Attribution and Chargeback System Across Business Units
questions.prompt: Ashbourne Telecom's AI platform serves twelve business units through shared model endpoints, and finance has no way to attribute cost to the business unit actually generating it -- the bill is one lump sum. Design and write the skeleton of a cost-attribution and chargeback system that tracks real per-request cost down to the business-unit level, including the parts that are genuinely hard to attribute cleanly.
questions.code:
// gateway_middleware.py -- every request through the shared gateway passes through this
def cost_attribution_middleware(request, call_next):
    business_unit = resolve_business_unit(request.api_key)  # never trust a client-supplied header
    request.context['business_unit'] = business_unit
    request.context['request_id'] = generate_request_id()
    start = time.monotonic()
    response = call_next(request)
    usage = extract_token_usage(response)  # input/output tokens, model version actually used
    cost_record = CostRecord(
        request_id=request.context['request_id'],
        business_unit=business_unit,
        model=usage.model_version,
        input_tokens=usage.input_tokens,
        output_tokens=usage.output_tokens,
        cost_usd=price_lookup(usage.model_version, usage.input_tokens, usage.output_tokens),
        shared_infra_flag=usage.used_shared_cache or usage.used_shared_retrieval_index,
        timestamp=now(),
    )
    cost_ledger.write(cost_record)
    return response

// monthly_chargeback_job.py
def compute_chargeback(month: str):
    direct_costs = cost_ledger.sum_by_business_unit(month, shared_infra_flag=False)
    shared_costs = cost_ledger.sum_by_business_unit(month, shared_infra_flag=True)
    shared_infra_overhead = infra_ledger.get_shared_overhead(month)  # GPU reservation, platform team cost
    total_direct_volume = cost_ledger.total_requests(month)
    for bu in business_units():
        bu_direct = direct_costs.get(bu, 0)
        bu_request_share = cost_ledger.request_count(month, bu) / total_direct_volume
        bu_shared_allocation = shared_infra_overhead * bu_request_share
        chargeback_ledger.write(bu, month, direct=bu_direct, shared_allocation=bu_shared_allocation)
questions.modelAnswer:
The straightforward part is direct per-request attribution: every request through the shared gateway carries an authenticated business-unit identity (resolved server-side from the API key, never trusted from a client-supplied header, since that's trivially spoofable), and the gateway middleware records the actual token usage and actual model version used for that specific request, since prices and token counts vary by model version and a chargeback system that assumes one flat rate per request will misattribute cost the moment a request gets routed to a different model tier than another superficially similar one.

The genuinely hard part is shared infrastructure cost that isn't cleanly attributable to a single request at all: reserved GPU capacity sized for aggregate baseline load across all twelve business units, a shared semantic cache or shared retrieval index whose existence benefits every business unit's latency and cost but isn't 'used' by one specific request in an attributable way, and the platform team's own engineering cost maintaining the shared gateway, none of which has a natural per-request cost. The design choice I'd make is to split the chargeback into two explicit components rather than forcing everything into one number: a direct cost component, which is exact and traceable to specific requests, and a shared-allocation component, which is necessarily an allocation, not a measurement -- I'd allocate shared infrastructure cost proportionally to each business unit's share of total request volume for the period, which is a defensible, auditable methodology even though it's an approximation, and I'd make that methodology visible to finance and to each business unit explicitly, rather than quietly blending allocated and direct cost into one number that looks more precise than it actually is.

The design principle underneath this: a chargeback system's credibility depends on business units being able to audit and trust the methodology, not just the final number, so every cost record traces back to a specific request with its actual token usage and model version, and every allocation is computed via a documented, consistent formula rather than a judgment call that changes month to month.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd split this into the easy half and the hard half, because treating them the same way is what makes chargeback systems lose credibility. The easy half is direct per-request cost -- every request through the gateway gets an authenticated business-unit identity resolved server-side, never trusted from a client header, and we record the actual token usage and actual model version for that specific call, because flat per-request pricing breaks the moment two superficially similar requests hit different model tiers.

The hard half is shared infrastructure -- reserved GPU capacity, a shared cache, the platform team's own time -- none of which has a clean per-request cost. I wouldn't try to force that into a fake precise number. I'd allocate it proportionally to each business unit's share of total request volume for the period, which is an honest, auditable approximation, and I'd report it as a clearly separate line item from direct cost, not blended into one number that looks more precise than it is.

The thing I actually care about most here is that finance and each business unit can audit the methodology itself, not just trust the final bill -- every direct cost record traces to a real request with real token usage, and every shared allocation follows one documented formula that doesn't change month to month without everyone knowing why.
questions.example: A concrete split: in a given month, Business Unit A generates $40,000 in direct, traceable cost from its own requests, plus a $6,000 proportional allocation of the $72,000 total shared GPU reservation overhead, based on A's 8.3% share of total platform request volume that month -- reported to A as two distinct, explained line items, not one merged $46,000 figure.
commonMistakes: Trusting a client-supplied header for business-unit identity instead of resolving it server-side from authentication
Assuming a flat per-request cost rather than tracking actual token usage and model version per request
Forcing shared infrastructure cost into a fake-precise per-request number instead of a transparent allocation
Blending direct and allocated cost into one figure instead of reporting them as separate, auditable line items
Changing the allocation methodology ad hoc month to month instead of using one documented, consistent formula
keyPoints: Business-unit identity is resolved server-side from authentication, never trusted from client input
Direct cost tracks actual token usage and actual model version per request, not a flat assumed rate
Shared infrastructure cost is allocated proportionally, reported as a distinct, clearly-labeled line item
Chargeback credibility depends on an auditable, consistent methodology businesses can verify, not just a final number

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Designs secure, server-side business-unit attribution per request
Tracks actual token usage and model version rather than a flat rate
Designs a defensible, transparent shared-cost allocation methodology
Separates direct and allocated cost as distinct, auditable line items
Code clarity

questions.title: Writing an Automated Red-Team Test Harness for Prompt Injection
questions.prompt: Longbridge Analytics ships new agent features monthly and currently relies on manual red-teaming before each launch, which doesn't scale and misses regressions when an unrelated change weakens an existing defense. Write the skeleton of an automated red-team test harness for prompt injection that runs continuously in CI, and explain how you'd keep its attack library current against real evolving techniques rather than stale canned test cases.
questions.modelAnswer:
The harness has to do two things manual red-teaming can't: run on every single change automatically, and detect regressions where an unrelated code change weakens a defense that used to hold. The skeleton structures each attack as a reusable, versioned test case with a payload generator, a category (direct injection in the user's own prompt, indirect injection smuggled in through retrieved content, multi-turn gradual escalation), a severity, and a detection function that inspects the actual agent transcript for evidence the injection succeeded -- not just whether the agent's final text output 'looks fine,' since a successful injection might succeed at getting a tool called with the wrong arguments even while producing an innocuous-looking final response. Running this as a required, blocking CI gate specifically on critical-severity bypasses, while still recording and trending every result (including lower-severity ones) is what catches the exact regression problem described: if a previously-blocked critical test case starts passing again after an unrelated change, the trend dashboard surfaces that immediately instead of waiting for the next scheduled manual red-team pass, which might be months away.

The harder problem is the attack library going stale, because real adversarial technique evolution doesn't wait for anyone's test-writing cadence. Keeping it current requires two separate feeds into the library, run on their own cadence rather than only at release time: pulling from external threat-intelligence sources that track emerging injection techniques across the industry, and -- just as important -- mining the company's own production incident history, since a successful real-world bypass that got caught after the fact is the single highest-signal source of a genuinely novel technique, and it should become a permanent regression test the moment it's understood, not just a one-time incident writeup. New candidate test cases from either feed go through human review before becoming part of the blocking gate, specifically because an automatically-synthesized test case with a buggy detection function could either produce false blocks that erode trust in the gate, or worse, silently fail to detect a real bypass while reporting a false pass.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd design this around two things manual red-teaming structurally can't do: run automatically on every single change, and catch the specific regression case described, where an unrelated change quietly weakens a defense that used to hold. Each attack becomes a versioned test case -- a payload generator, a category like direct injection versus indirect injection through retrieved content versus multi-turn escalation, a severity, and a detection function that actually inspects the agent's behavior and tool calls, not just whether the final text output looks okay, because a successful injection can get the wrong tool called with the wrong arguments while still producing an innocuous-sounding response.

I'd make critical-severity bypasses a hard CI gate, but record every result, including lower-severity ones, into a trend dashboard, because the regression case they're worried about shows up exactly there -- a test case that used to reliably block now starts passing, and that should surface immediately in CI, not at the next scheduled manual pass months later.

For keeping the library current, I'd treat that as a separate, ongoing process from CI itself: pull from external threat-intel feeds tracking emerging injection techniques, and just as importantly, mine our own production incidents -- any real bypass that got caught in the wild is the single best source of a genuinely novel technique, and it should become a permanent regression test the moment we understand it, not just a postmortem writeup that gets filed away. Every new candidate test case goes through human review before it's trusted as a blocking gate, because a badly-written detection function is worse than no test at all -- it gives false confidence.
questions.example: A concrete catch: a refactor of the agent's tool-execution layer unintentionally removes an argument-sanitization step; the next CI run on an unrelated feature branch re-runs the full attack library and a previously-blocked indirect-injection test case that exploits exactly that missing sanitization starts passing again, blocking the deploy before it ever reaches production.
commonMistakes: Detecting a successful injection only by inspecting the final text output rather than actual tool calls/behavior
Running red-team tests only before major releases instead of continuously in CI on every change
Treating the attack library as a static, one-time artifact instead of refreshing it from threat intel and real incidents
Automatically promoting newly synthesized test cases into the blocking gate without human review
Not trending lower-severity results over time, missing the exact 'used to block, now passes' regression signal
keyPoints: Detection functions inspect actual agent behavior and tool calls, not just surface-level final text output
Critical bypasses block CI; all results feed a trend dashboard to catch regressions in previously-blocked cases
The attack library is refreshed continuously from external threat intel and from the company's own production incidents
New candidate test cases require human review before becoming part of the blocking gate
Running continuously in CI, not just before major releases, is what catches defense regressions from unrelated changes

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Designs detection based on actual behavior/tool calls, not surface output alone
Correctly structures the CI gate to block critical bypasses while trending all results
Designs a concrete, ongoing attack-library refresh process from real sources
Requires human review before new test cases become blocking
Code clarity

questions.title: Implementing a Model-Rollback Orchestrator with Staged Traffic Shifting
questions.prompt: Foxglove Health needs the ability to roll back a bad model deployment within minutes, with evidence-based confidence rather than a panicked all-or-nothing flip. Write the skeleton of a model-rollback orchestrator that shifts traffic in stages, monitors health signals at each stage, and automatically rolls back if those signals degrade -- and explain the decisions that make this safe to trust during an actual incident.
questions.modelAnswer:
An all-or-nothing flip means the worst case -- a bad model serving 100% of traffic -- happens immediately on deploy, with no window to catch it before every user is affected. Staged traffic shifting bounds that worst case deliberately: starting at 1% means a genuinely bad deployment only ever affects a small fraction of traffic before the health checks at that stage catch it, and the stage progression (1%, 5%, 25%, 50%, 100% in the skeleton) means each subsequent stage's blast radius if something goes wrong grows gradually rather than jumping straight to full exposure. Each stage holds for a fixed dwell time, not just an instant, specifically because some regressions (a slow memory leak, a quality degradation that only shows up under sustained load, a rare edge case that needs enough request volume to surface statistically) wouldn't be visible in a one-second check immediately after the traffic shift -- the dwell time is what gives real health signals a chance to actually accumulate before advancing.

The health checks themselves need to cover more than raw error rate, because a model can be 'working' in the sense of returning valid responses while quietly degrading in ways that matter more -- judge-score quality, latency percentiles (not just averages, since a shift in the tail is often the first sign of trouble under load), and escalation rate (how often the system is handing off to a human or an error path) are all signals that catch different failure modes raw error rate alone would miss. Automatic rollback firing the moment any watched signal breaches its threshold, without requiring a human to notice and decide, is what makes 'rollback within minutes' actually achievable rather than aspirational, since a human noticing a dashboard anomaly and deciding to act is reliably slower than an automated check running every ten seconds.

What makes this trustworthy during a real incident is that every stage transition and every rollback decision is logged with the specific reason and the specific stage it happened at, so after an incident, there's a concrete, reconstructable record of exactly what the system observed and when, rather than relying on someone's memory of what the dashboard looked like at 3am -- that audit trail is also what lets the team calibrate the health-check thresholds over time based on real data about which thresholds caught real problems versus which triggered unnecessary rollbacks.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The whole point of staging is bounding the worst case -- an all-or-nothing flip means a bad model immediately hits 100% of users with zero window to catch it, while starting at 1% and climbing means a genuinely bad deployment only ever touches a small slice before the health checks catch it. I'd hold each stage for a real dwell time, not just check instantaneously right after the traffic shift, because some regressions -- a slow leak, quality degradation that only shows up under real load -- need actual time and volume to become visible.

For the health checks, I wouldn't just watch error rate -- I'd watch judge-score quality, latency at the tail percentiles rather than just the average, and escalation rate, because a model can look fine on raw error rate while quietly degrading on every signal that actually matters to users. And I'd make the rollback automatic the instant any of those breach, with no human in the loop to notice and decide, because a person watching a dashboard is reliably slower than a check running every ten seconds, and 'rollback within minutes' only actually happens if the system does it itself.

The thing that makes this trustworthy after the fact is the audit trail -- every stage advance and every rollback gets logged with exactly what triggered it and at what stage, so a postmortem has a real, reconstructable record instead of someone's fuzzy memory of a 3am dashboard, and that same record is what lets us calibrate the thresholds over time based on which ones actually caught real problems.
questions.example: A concrete run: a candidate model advances cleanly through 1% and 5%, but at the 25% stage, latency p99 crosses its threshold after the dwell window accumulates enough traffic to surface a performance regression that wasn't visible at 5% volume; the orchestrator automatically rolls back to the baseline and flags the exact stage and metric, rather than the regression surfacing for the first time at 100%.
commonMistakes: Checking health signals only instantaneously right after a traffic shift instead of over a real dwell window
Watching only raw error rate instead of quality, latency-tail, and escalation-rate signals together
Requiring a human to notice and manually trigger rollback instead of automating it on threshold breach
Jumping stages too aggressively (e.g. 1% straight to 50%), undermining the bounded-blast-radius purpose of staging
Not logging the specific reason and stage for each rollback, losing the record needed for postmortems and threshold calibration
keyPoints: Staged traffic shifting bounds the worst-case blast radius of a bad deployment instead of exposing all traffic at once
Each stage holds for a real dwell time so regressions needing sustained load or volume have a chance to surface
Health checks cover quality, latency-tail, and escalation-rate signals, not just raw error rate
Rollback triggers automatically on threshold breach rather than waiting on human detection
A full audit trail of stage transitions and rollback reasons supports postmortems and threshold calibration

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the bounded-blast-radius rationale for staged rollout
Designs health checks covering multiple relevant signal types, not just error rate
Designs automatic rollback rather than human-dependent detection
Includes a dwell-time mechanism and full audit trail

questions.title: Writing a Data-Lineage Tracker for RAG Source Documents
questions.prompt: Sterling Cross Bank's compliance team can't currently answer 'which production AI responses were generated using this specific document' when a source document turns out to be outdated or incorrect, which blocks any targeted remediation. Write the skeleton of a data-lineage tracker for a RAG pipeline that makes this traceable end to end, and explain the design choices that keep it accurate without adding unacceptable latency to every request.
questions.code:
// lineage_tracker.py
class LineageRecord:
    def __init__(self, request_id, retrieved_chunks, model_version, response_hash, timestamp):
        self.request_id = request_id
        self.retrieved_chunks = retrieved_chunks  # list of (doc_id, doc_version, chunk_id, similarity_score)
        self.model_version = model_version
        self.response_hash = response_hash
        self.timestamp = timestamp

def rag_pipeline_with_lineage(query, request_id):
    retrieved = retriever.search(query)  # returns chunks WITH doc_id + doc_version metadata already attached
    context = build_context(retrieved)
    response = model.generate(query, context, )
    record = LineageRecord(
        request_id=request_id,
        retrieved_chunks=[(c.doc_id, c.doc_version, c.chunk_id, c.score) for c in retrieved],
        model_version=model.version,
        response_hash=hash(response),
        timestamp=now(),
    )
    lineage_store.write(record)  # append-only, indexed by doc_id AND by request_id
    return response

// compliance_query.py
def find_responses_using_document(doc_id: str, doc_version: str | None = None):
    # Indexed lookup: doc_id -> all request_ids that retrieved any chunk of it
    records = lineage_store.query_by_doc(doc_id, doc_version)
    return [r.request_id for r in records]
questions.modelAnswer:
The question compliance needs answered -- which responses used this document -- is unanswerable after the fact unless every single retrieval event records exactly which document, which version of that document, and which specific chunk contributed to that response's context, at the moment the request happened, not reconstructed later from logs that weren't designed for this. The skeleton captures that at the one point in the pipeline where it's cheap and natural to capture: the retriever already knows exactly which chunks it returned and from which documents, so attaching doc_id, doc_version, and chunk_id to each retrieved chunk as metadata that already exists in the retrieval index, and writing a lineage record immediately after retrieval, adds no extra retrieval call and no extra model call -- it's purely recording information the pipeline already has in hand.

The doc_version field matters specifically for the compliance scenario described: if a document gets updated, the lineage record needs to distinguish 'this response used version 3 of the policy document' from 'this response used version 4,' because the remediation question compliance is actually asking is almost always version-specific -- version 3 was wrong, was it fixed before or after this specific response was generated. Indexing the lineage store by doc_id (and doc_version) in addition to request_id is what makes the compliance query fast and direct rather than requiring a full scan of every lineage record ever written -- a document-centric index answers 'which requests used this document' in one indexed lookup instead of a linear search.

The latency concern is real but solvable without sacrificing accuracy: the lineage write happens after the response is already being returned to the user, as a fire-and-forget append to a store optimized for high write-throughput, not a synchronous step the user's request waits on, and because it only records metadata the retriever already produced rather than computing anything new, the write itself is small and fast. The one thing I would not compromise on for latency reasons is completeness -- every single retrieval, not a sampled subset, gets a lineage record, because a compliance tool that only has visibility into some fraction of production traffic can't actually answer 'which responses used this document' with any confidence, it can only answer 'which of the responses we happened to sample.'
questions.professionalAnswer:
The question compliance is actually asking -- which responses used this specific document -- is only answerable if every retrieval event records exactly which document, which version, and which chunk fed into that response's context, captured at the moment it happened. The good news is the retriever already knows this; it's not new information we have to compute, it's metadata already sitting in the retrieval index. So I'd attach doc_id, doc_version, and chunk_id to every retrieved chunk and write a lineage record right after retrieval, which doesn't cost an extra retrieval call or an extra model call.

The doc_version field is the detail I'd insist on, because the real compliance question is almost always version-specific -- was this response generated from the version of the policy that was wrong, or the version after it was fixed. And I'd index the lineage store by document, not just by request, because without that index, 'which requests used this document' means scanning every lineage record ever written instead of one direct lookup.

For latency, I'd make the write fire-and-forget after the response is already on its way back to the user, into a store built for high write throughput, since it's just recording metadata the pipeline already produced. The one thing I wouldn't compromise on is coverage -- every retrieval gets a record, not a sampled subset, because a compliance answer based on a sample isn't actually an answer to 'which responses used this document,' it's an answer to 'which of the ones we happened to log.'
questions.example: A concrete remediation flow: compliance flags that policy document 'refund-policy-v3.pdf' contained an incorrect clause between March 1 and March 14; a single indexed lineage query for doc_id='refund-policy' with that version returns the exact 340 production responses generated using that specific version in that window, giving a precise remediation list instead of an estimate.
commonMistakes: Logging only document-level references without tracking the specific document version used
Making the lineage write a synchronous step the user's request has to wait on
Indexing the lineage store only by request_id, forcing a full scan to answer document-centric compliance queries
Sampling lineage records instead of recording every single retrieval event
Treating lineage capture as a separate reconstruction effort instead of recording metadata the retriever already produces
keyPoints: Lineage records capture doc_id, doc_version, and chunk_id for every retrieved chunk at the moment of retrieval
Document-version-level tracking is what makes version-specific remediation questions answerable
The lineage store is indexed by document as well as by request, enabling direct compliance queries
Lineage writes are fire-and-forget after the response is already returned, avoiding added user-facing latency
Every retrieval event is recorded, not a sampled subset, since compliance needs complete coverage

Designs an index that supports direct document-centric compliance queries
Avoids adding synchronous latency to the user-facing request
Insists on complete coverage rather than sampling for a compliance use case

questions.title: Implementing an Audit-Log Pipeline for SOC2 / EU AI Act Record-Keeping
questions.prompt: Thackeray Legal needs its AI platform's audit logging to satisfy both SOC2 evidence requirements and the EU AI Act's record-keeping obligations for a high-risk AI system, and the current logging is inconsistent across services. Write the skeleton of a unified audit-log pipeline that meets both, and explain what each regime actually requires that a generic application log doesn't already provide.
questions.code:
// audit_event.py -- the canonical schema every service emits through, not its own ad-hoc log format
class AIAuditEvent:
    def __init__(self, event_id, request_id, timestamp, actor, system_id, system_version,
                 input_summary, output_summary, decision_basis, human_override, retention_tier):
        self.event_id = event_id
        self.request_id = request_id
        self.timestamp = timestamp
        self.actor = actor                    # authenticated user or service identity, never anonymous
        self.system_id = system_id            # which AI system/feature generated this
        self.system_version = system_version  # exact model + prompt-template version
        self.input_summary = input_summary    # redacted/hashed where raw input is sensitive
        self.output_summary = output_summary
        self.decision_basis = decision_basis  # e.g. retrieved sources, confidence score, rule triggered
        self.human_override = human_override  # was this reviewed/overridden by a human, and by whom
        self.retention_tier = retention_tier  # drives retention duration per regulatory requirement

def emit_audit_event(event: AIAuditEvent):
    validate_schema(event)  # reject anything missing a required field -- no silent partial logs
    immutable_store.append(event)  # write-once, tamper-evident (hash-chained) storage
    if event.retention_tier == 'high_risk_ai_act':
        retention_scheduler.register(event.event_id, min_years=10)
    audit_index.index(event)  # queryable by system_id, actor, date range, and decision_basis
questions.modelAnswer:
A generic application log is built to help an engineer debug a specific incident, which means it's typically mutable, inconsistently structured across services, often omits exactly the fields a compliance regime cares about (who made the decision, what it was based on, whether a human reviewed it), and has no enforced retention guarantee -- any of which can be true without anyone noticing until an audit asks for something the logs don't have. SOC2 evidence requirements care primarily about demonstrating that access controls, change management, and monitoring actually operated as designed over the audit period, which means the audit trail needs to prove who did what, when, under what authenticated identity, consistently enough across every system in scope that an auditor can sample it and trust the sample represents the whole. The EU AI Act's record-keeping obligation for a high-risk AI system goes further and is specific to the AI system's own decision-making: it requires retaining enough information to reconstruct why the system produced a given output -- the exact model and prompt-template version in effect, the basis for the decision (retrieved sources, confidence signals, which rule or classification fired), and whether a human reviewed or overrode it -- for a defined minimum retention period, specifically because the regulatory concern is being able to reconstruct and justify an automated decision months or years later, not just prove general system hygiene.

The skeleton's canonical schema is the structural answer to the inconsistency problem: every service emits through the same AIAuditEvent shape rather than its own ad-hoc log format, with schema validation rejecting anything missing a required field, since a compliance audit trail with silent gaps is often worse than no audit trail at all, because it creates false confidence that evidence exists. Immutable, hash-chained storage addresses a requirement generic logs don't carry at all: both regimes care about tamper-evidence, not just existence, since a log an engineer (or an attacker) could quietly edit after the fact doesn't actually prove anything happened the way the record claims. The retention_tier field and the dedicated retention scheduler exist because the two regimes have different, specific retention requirements, and treating retention as a per-event, enforced property (not a generic 'keep logs for 90 days and rotate' default most logging infrastructure ships with) is what actually satisfies a ten-year EU AI Act retention requirement for a high-risk system rather than quietly losing the evidence to a storage-cost-driven rotation policy nobody flagged as a compliance risk.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd start by naming what a generic application log is actually built for -- helping an engineer debug something -- and why that's a different job than what either compliance regime needs. SOC2 cares about proving access control, change management, and monitoring actually worked as designed over a period, consistently enough across every system that an auditor can sample it and trust the sample. The EU AI Act's record-keeping requirement for a high-risk system goes further and is specific to the AI decision itself -- it wants enough to reconstruct why the system produced a given output months or years later: the exact model and prompt version, what the decision was based on, whether a human reviewed it.

So the fix isn't 'log more' -- it's a canonical event schema every service emits through, with schema validation that rejects anything missing a required field, because a compliance trail with silent gaps is arguably worse than having no trail at all, it just creates false confidence. I'd make the store immutable and hash-chained, because both regimes care about tamper-evidence, not just existence -- a log someone could quietly edit after the fact doesn't actually prove the thing it claims to prove. And I'd make retention a per-event, enforced property tied to the specific regulatory requirement that event falls under, not a generic rotation policy, because a ten-year EU AI Act retention requirement getting silently cut short by a storage-cost-driven log rotation policy is exactly the kind of gap that only gets discovered during an actual audit, which is the worst possible time.
questions.example: A concrete gap this closes: a loan-underwriting decision made eighteen months ago gets challenged, and compliance needs to reconstruct exactly which model version made the call and what it was based on -- with the unified pipeline, a single indexed query on request_id returns the exact system_version, decision_basis, and human_override fields; with the prior ad-hoc per-service logging, that information had already rotated out of three of the four services involved.
commonMistakes: Treating generic application logs as sufficient for compliance evidence without the fields each regime actually requires
Using mutable log storage with no tamper-evidence for an audit trail that needs to prove what actually happened
Applying one generic retention/rotation policy instead of a per-event retention tier matched to the actual regulatory requirement
Allowing services to log in inconsistent ad-hoc formats instead of a validated canonical schema
Logging the decision outcome without the decision basis (sources, confidence, rule triggered) the EU AI Act actually requires
keyPoints: SOC2 needs consistent, sampleable evidence that access control and monitoring operated as designed
The EU AI Act's record-keeping obligation needs reconstructable decision basis, system version, and human-override status
A canonical, schema-validated event format replaces inconsistent ad-hoc per-service logging
Immutable, tamper-evident storage is required because both regimes care about proof, not just existence
Retention must be an enforced, per-event property matched to the specific regulatory requirement, not a generic rotation default

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes what SOC2 and the EU AI Act each specifically require
Designs a canonical, validated event schema replacing ad-hoc logging
Designs immutable, tamper-evident storage
Designs enforced, regime-specific retention rather than a generic policy

questions.title: Designing a Secrets Management Layer for Agent Tool Credentials
questions.prompt: Oakhaven Freight's agents call a growing number of internal and external tools, each needing its own credentials, and several API keys have ended up hardcoded directly in agent configuration files that get checked into the repository. Write the skeleton of a secrets management layer purpose-built for agent tool access, and explain the specific risks that make this different from ordinary application secrets management.
questions.modelAnswer:
Ordinary application secrets management assumes the code paths using a credential are fixed and reviewed in advance -- a service's own source code decides exactly when and how an API key gets used, so scoping and auditing a secret mostly means controlling which service can access it at all. An LLM-driven agent breaks that assumption in a specific way: the agent itself decides, at runtime, when to invoke a tool and with what arguments, driven by model-generated reasoning that can be influenced by adversarial input (prompt injection) or simple model error, which means the actual risk isn't just 'which service can access this secret,' it's 'what can the model, potentially manipulated, actually do with this secret once it's invoked a tool call.' That reframes the whole design: credentials issued to an agent need to be scoped as narrowly as the specific tool call actually requires, issued short-lived rather than long-lived, since a long-lived broad credential handed to an agent is a standing exposure for every future prompt injection attempt against that agent, not just the current request.

The design in the skeleton reflects that reframing in two specific ways beyond standard secrets management. First, per-agent, per-tool, per-scope policy enforcement at the moment of issuance: the credential provider checks the requesting agent's identity and the specific scope requested against an explicit allow-list before issuing anything, rather than handing out a broad, multi-purpose credential once and trusting the agent (or the model generating its behavior) to only use the parts of it that are appropriate. Second, and this is the detail that's genuinely different from ordinary secrets management: the credential itself must never enter the LLM's own context window or transcript, because anything that ends up in context is something the model could, in principle, be manipulated into revealing, repeating, or reasoning about in its own generated text -- the tool executor retrieves and uses the credential in the surrounding orchestration code, outside the boundary of what the model itself ever sees or generates, so even a fully successful prompt injection that convinces the model to try to exfiltrate a secret has no secret value sitting in its own context to exfiltrate.

Every credential issuance is logged with the requesting agent identity, the tool, the scope, and the TTL, specifically because after an incident, the question 'what could this agent have actually done with the credentials it held during this window' needs to be answerable precisely, not reconstructed from application logs that were never designed to answer a security question.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The thing that's actually different here versus ordinary secrets management is who decides when a credential gets used. In a normal service, the code decides, and that code is fixed and reviewed in advance. With an agent, the model itself decides at runtime whether to invoke a tool and with what arguments, and that decision can be influenced by a prompt injection or just a model mistake -- so the real question isn't just 'which service can access this secret,' it's 'what could a manipulated model actually do with it once a tool call happens.'

That changes the design in two specific ways. First, I'd scope and issue credentials per-agent, per-tool, per-scope, short-lived, checked against an explicit policy at the moment of issuance -- never a broad, long-lived key handed out once, because that's a standing exposure to every future injection attempt against that agent, not just the current request. Second, and this is the detail I'd insist on: the credential itself should never enter the model's own context window or transcript. The tool executor should fetch and use it in the surrounding orchestration code, outside anything the model ever sees or generates, so even a fully successful injection that convinces the model to try to leak a secret has no actual secret sitting in its context to leak.

And every single issuance gets logged with the agent identity, tool, scope, and TTL, because after any incident, I want to be able to answer precisely what this specific agent could have done during a specific window, not reconstruct it from logs that were never built to answer that question.
questions.example: A concrete prevention: an attacker's prompt injection convinces the claims agent to try printing its own credentials into a chat response to exfiltrate them -- because the credential was never placed in the agent's context in the first place, there's nothing for the model to print; the injection succeeds at manipulating the model's text output but fails to exfiltrate anything of value.
commonMistakes: Issuing broad, long-lived credentials to an agent instead of narrowly scoped, short-lived ones per tool call
Placing the actual credential value into the model's context window where a prompt injection could try to extract it
Treating agent secrets management the same as ordinary service secrets management without accounting for runtime model decision-making
Not logging per-issuance detail (agent identity, tool, scope, TTL) needed to answer 'what could this agent have done' after an incident
Hardcoding credentials in agent configuration files instead of issuing them dynamically through a scoped provider
keyPoints: Agents differ from ordinary services because the model decides at runtime when and how to use a credential
Credentials should be scoped narrowly per tool call and issued short-lived, not broad and long-lived
The credential value must never enter the model's own context window, so a successful injection can't exfiltrate it
Per-issuance policy enforcement checks agent identity, tool, and scope against an explicit allow-list
Detailed issuance logging answers 'what could this agent have done' precisely after an incident

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies why agent secrets management differs from ordinary service secrets management
Designs narrow scoping and short-lived issuance per tool call
Designs keeping the credential value out of the model's context window
Designs adequate audit logging for post-incident reconstruction

questions.title: Writing a Rate-Limiter and Circuit-Breaker for a Shared LLM Gateway
questions.prompt: Hartwell Robotics' shared LLM gateway has no protection against one misbehaving or runaway consumer starving capacity for every other team, and a recent incident saw one team's buggy retry loop degrade latency platform-wide. Write the skeleton of a rate-limiter and circuit-breaker layered on the shared gateway that protects the platform without punishing well-behaved consumers for someone else's bug.
questions.modelAnswer:
The incident happened because the gateway had no isolation between consumers -- one team's retry storm consumed shared capacity (connection slots, upstream rate-limit budget, queueing capacity) that every other team was also drawing from, so a bug in one team's code became a latency problem for teams with perfectly correct code. The fix requires two distinct mechanisms doing two distinct jobs. The rate-limiter enforces a per-consumer budget (requests per second and concurrent in-flight requests, in the skeleton) so that even a consumer sending a genuinely broken, high-volume retry loop hits their own ceiling and gets rejected past it, rather than consuming capacity that was never allocated to them -- this is what directly prevents the specific incident described, since the buggy retry loop would have been capped at its own consumer's limit instead of degrading the shared upstream for everyone.

The circuit breaker solves a different, related problem: protecting the platform from a failing upstream dependency itself, independent of any single consumer's behavior. If the model provider or a specific upstream endpoint starts failing at a high rate, continuing to send it traffic at full volume just wastes capacity on calls that are statistically very likely to fail anyway, and can make the upstream's own recovery slower by adding more load to an already-struggling system. Tripping open after a failure-rate threshold within a rolling window, rejecting calls fast during the open state instead of letting them time out slowly, and probing with a half-open state after a cooldown rather than immediately resuming full traffic, is what lets the platform fail fast and recover gracefully instead of either hammering a failing upstream indefinitely or requiring a human to notice and intervene.

The design choice that specifically protects well-behaved consumers from someone else's bug is per-consumer scoping on the rate limiter (not a single shared platform-wide limit that one bad actor can exhaust on behalf of everyone) combined with the circuit breaker operating per-upstream-dependency rather than per-consumer, since the failing dependency is shared infrastructure, but the retry-storm problem is consumer-specific -- conflating the two into one mechanism would either let a misbehaving consumer still degrade shared capacity (if only a circuit breaker existed) or fail to protect against a genuinely failing upstream (if only per-consumer limiting existed).
questions.professionalAnswer:
The root cause of the incident is that there was no isolation between consumers -- one team's bug consumed shared capacity that every other team was also drawing from, so their bug became everyone's latency problem. I'd fix that with a per-consumer rate limit, both requests-per-second and concurrent in-flight requests, so even a genuinely broken retry loop hits its own ceiling and gets rejected past it, instead of consuming capacity it was never allocated.

That's a different problem from protecting the platform against a failing upstream dependency itself, which is what the circuit breaker is for -- if the model provider starts failing at a high rate, continuing to send full volume just wastes capacity on calls that are likely to fail anyway and can slow the upstream's own recovery. I'd trip it open on a rolling failure-rate threshold, fail fast during the open state instead of letting calls time out slowly, and probe with a half-open state after a cooldown rather than immediately dumping full traffic back.

The key design decision that actually prevents a repeat of this specific incident is keeping these two mechanisms scoped differently -- rate limiting per consumer, circuit breaking per upstream dependency -- because the retry-storm problem is consumer-specific and the failing-dependency problem is shared infrastructure. Conflating them into one mechanism either lets a bad consumer still degrade shared capacity, or fails to protect against a genuinely failing upstream.
questions.example: Replaying the incident with this in place: the buggy retry loop sends requests at ten times its allocated concurrency limit; the limiter rejects everything past that ceiling for that one consumer specifically, and every other team's requests continue flowing through the gateway at normal latency, unaffected.
commonMistakes: Enforcing one shared platform-wide rate limit instead of per-consumer limits that isolate one team's bug from another
Conflating rate limiting (consumer-specific) and circuit breaking (upstream-dependency-specific) into one mechanism
Letting the circuit breaker immediately resume full traffic after cooldown instead of probing with a half-open state
Letting failed calls time out slowly instead of failing fast once the circuit is open
Not scoping concurrency limits in addition to raw request-rate limits, missing a common runaway-retry failure mode
keyPoints: Per-consumer rate limiting isolates one team's bug or retry storm from degrading shared capacity for everyone else
A circuit breaker protects the platform from a failing upstream dependency, a distinct problem from consumer misbehavior
The circuit breaker fails fast during the open state and probes with a half-open state before resuming full traffic
Rate limiting is scoped per consumer; circuit breaking is scoped per upstream dependency -- conflating them weakens both protections
Concurrency limits, not just requests-per-second, are needed to catch retry-storm-style failures

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses the incident as a consumer-isolation failure
Designs per-consumer rate limiting with both rate and concurrency dimensions
Designs a correct circuit-breaker state machine (closed/open/half-open) for upstream protection
Correctly separates the scoping of the two mechanisms
Code clarity

questions.title: Building a Golden-Dataset Regression Harness with Statistical Significance
questions.prompt: Cold Spring Capital's team currently decides whether a prompt change is safe to ship by comparing two raw average scores and shipping if the new number is higher. Write the skeleton of a proper golden-dataset regression harness that applies real statistical significance testing before approving a change, and explain exactly what was wrong with the raw-average approach.
questions.modelAnswer:
Comparing two raw averages and shipping whenever the new number is higher ignores the fact that both numbers are estimates with real sampling uncertainty, not exact measurements -- a new average that's higher by less than the natural run-to-run variance of the eval set tells you essentially nothing about whether the change actually improved anything, and shipping on that basis means roughly half the time a genuinely neutral or even slightly negative change will show a higher raw average purely by chance and get shipped as an 'improvement.' The fix the skeleton implements is a paired significance test (a paired t-test, since the same golden examples are scored under both the baseline and the candidate, which is a more statistically powerful comparison than treating them as independent samples) plus a confidence interval on the actual difference, which answers the real question -- not 'is the new number bigger,' but 'how confident are we that there's a real difference, and how big is that difference likely to actually be.'

The part that's easy to skip and genuinely important is the power check before even running the significance test: if the golden set doesn't have enough examples to reliably detect a meaningful effect size (defined here as min_detectable_effect, the smallest change the team actually cares about catching), then a 'no significant difference' result from an underpowered test is not evidence of no difference, it's evidence that the test couldn't have detected a difference even if one existed. The harness's ship_decision function reflects that directly: an INSUFFICIENT_POWER verdict blocks the ship, the same as an actual detected regression, because approving a change on the basis of a test that structurally couldn't have caught a regression is functionally the same mistake as ignoring significance testing altogether, just dressed up in statistical language that looks more rigorous than it is.

The bootstrap confidence interval on the mean difference adds the piece a p-value alone doesn't give: even a statistically significant result can correspond to a practically tiny effect size that doesn't matter for the business, and the confidence interval is what lets a human reviewer see the actual plausible range of the real effect, not just whether it cleared an arbitrary significance threshold -- a p-value under 0.05 attached to a confidence interval of [0.001, 0.004] on a 0-1 score scale is a very different ship decision than the same p-value attached to [0.03, 0.09].
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd name exactly what's wrong with raw-average comparison: both numbers are estimates with real sampling noise, and if the new number is higher by less than that natural noise, you've learned nothing -- roughly half the time, a genuinely neutral change will show a higher raw average purely by chance, and shipping on that basis means you're shipping noise as if it were signal about half the time it happens.

What I'd build instead is a paired significance test -- paired specifically because the same golden examples get scored under both versions, which is a more powerful comparison than treating the two runs as independent -- plus a confidence interval on the actual size of the difference, because the real question isn't 'is the new number bigger,' it's 'how confident are we there's a real difference, and roughly how big is it.'

The piece I'd insist on that's easy to skip is a power check before trusting any 'no significant difference' result. If the golden set doesn't have enough examples to reliably detect the effect size we actually care about catching, a 'no difference' result isn't evidence of no difference -- it's evidence the test couldn't have caught a real regression even if one existed. So in my ship-decision logic, insufficient power blocks the ship exactly like a detected regression does, because approving on an underpowered test is the same underlying mistake as skipping significance testing, just with more decimal places.
questions.example: A concrete contrast: baseline mean 0.871, candidate mean 0.879 -- the raw-average approach ships this as an improvement; a paired significance test on the same 40-example golden set returns p=0.41 with a confidence interval on the difference spanning [-0.02, 0.04], meaning the data can't actually distinguish this from pure noise, and the correct verdict is NO_SIGNIFICANT_CHANGE, not a shipped improvement.
commonMistakes: Shipping whenever the new raw average is numerically higher, ignoring sampling noise entirely
Running an independent-samples test instead of a paired test when the same examples are scored under both versions
Treating a 'no significant difference' result from an underpowered test as evidence of no real difference
Reporting only a p-value with no confidence interval, missing whether a significant effect is actually practically meaningful
Not defining a minimum detectable effect size in advance, making the power check impossible to apply meaningfully
keyPoints: Raw-average comparison ignores sampling noise and can ship a neutral or negative change as an 'improvement' by chance
A paired significance test is the correct comparison when the same golden examples are scored under both versions
A power check must run before trusting a 'no significant difference' result as real evidence
A confidence interval on the effect size, not just a p-value, is needed to judge practical significance
Insufficient statistical power should block a ship decision the same way a detected regression does

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains why raw-average comparison is statistically unsound
Designs a correct paired significance test with confidence interval
Designs a power check that blocks ship decisions on underpowered tests
Code clarity

questions.title: Designing a Multi-Tenant Prompt-Template Versioning System
questions.prompt: Fennimore Retail's platform serves prompt templates to dozens of internal consumers, and right now editing a shared template directly in production has already caused one team's feature to silently break when another team changed wording they both depended on. Write the skeleton of a multi-tenant prompt-template versioning system that prevents this, and explain the design principle that makes shared templates safe to evolve.
questions.modelAnswer:
The incident happened because the template was mutable in place and consumption was implicit -- every consumer was effectively pinned to 'whatever the current content of this template happens to be right now,' with no version boundary between a change one team intends and the behavior every other dependent team actually experiences. The design principle that fixes this is the same one that makes shared library versioning safe in ordinary software: publish immutable versions, never edit a version's content in place, and require every consumer to explicitly pin which version they depend on rather than silently riding whatever is 'latest.' In the skeleton, publish() always creates a new version rather than mutating an existing one, and resolve() refuses to serve a template to a consumer with no explicit pin at all -- there's deliberately no implicit 'give me the newest version' default, because that default is exactly the mechanism that caused the original incident.

This alone would make shared templates safe but frozen, which creates a different problem -- templates could never evolve without every consumer manually re-pinning, which doesn't scale either. The eval-gate inside publish() is what makes evolution possible without reintroducing the risk: a new version has to pass the eval suite associated with that template before it's even allowed to exist as a publishable version, which catches a meaningful fraction of actually-breaking changes before any consumer could even choose to adopt them, and because pinning is explicit, a consumer adopting a new version is always a deliberate decision made by that consumer's own team, at a time they choose, rather than something that happens to them because someone else edited shared content.
