The deprecate() flow closes the remaining gap: an old version doesn't just get silently removed once nobody expects to be using it, it goes through an explicit notification to every consumer still pinned to it, with a defined sunset date, so a team that never got around to upgrading isn't surprised by removal any more than they were previously surprised by an in-place edit -- the registry always knows exactly which consumers depend on which version, because that dependency is tracked explicitly rather than inferred, which is the same property that made the cost-attribution and dependency-registry designs elsewhere on this platform work: you can't manage a dependency safely if the system doesn't actually know it exists.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The incident is a version-boundary problem -- the template was mutable in place, and every consumer was implicitly pinned to 'whatever this template currently says,' with no boundary between a change one team makes and the behavior every other dependent team experiences. I'd fix this the same way shared library versioning gets fixed in ordinary software: publish immutable versions, never edit a version's content after the fact, and require every consumer to explicitly pin a version rather than silently riding 'latest' by default.

But frozen versions alone create a different problem -- nothing can evolve without every consumer manually re-pinning, which doesn't scale. So I'd gate publishing a new version behind that template's own eval suite, which catches a real fraction of breaking changes before any consumer could even adopt them, and because pinning is always explicit, adopting a new version becomes a deliberate choice each team makes on their own timeline, not something that happens to them.

And for deprecating an old version, I wouldn't just quietly remove it once it looks unused -- I'd notify every consumer still pinned to it with a defined sunset date, because a team that never upgraded shouldn't get blindsided by removal any more than they were previously blindsided by an in-place edit. The whole thing works because the registry always knows explicitly which consumers depend on which version -- you can't manage a shared dependency safely if the system doesn't actually track that it exists.
questions.example: A concrete prevention: Team A wants to tighten the wording in a shared template; they publish version 14, which passes the eval suite; Team B, still explicitly pinned to version 12, experiences zero behavior change, and only adopts version 14 when they choose to re-pin after validating it against their own use case.
commonMistakes: Editing a shared template's content in place instead of publishing a new immutable version
Letting consumers implicitly ride a 'latest' version instead of requiring an explicit pin
Allowing a new version to publish without passing a regression eval gate
Removing an old version without notifying and giving a sunset date to consumers still pinned to it
Not tracking which consumers depend on which specific version explicitly
keyPoints: Templates are published as immutable versions, never edited in place
Consumers explicitly pin a specific version; there is no implicit 'latest' default
New versions are gated behind that template's own eval suite before they can be published
Deprecating an old version requires explicit notification and a sunset date for consumers still pinned to it
Explicit, tracked consumer-to-version dependency is what makes safe evolution possible

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses the incident as a mutable-content, implicit-dependency problem
Designs immutable versioning with explicit consumer pinning
Designs an eval gate enabling safe template evolution
Designs a notification-based deprecation flow
Code clarity

questions.title: Building a PII Redaction Pipeline for Vector Store Ingestion
questions.prompt: Cragmoor Freight is ingesting customer support transcripts into a vector store for RAG, and a privacy review found unredacted customer names, phone numbers, and partial account numbers embedded directly into stored chunks, now retrievable by any agent session that happens to match on them. Write the skeleton of a PII redaction pipeline for vector-store ingestion, and explain why this has to happen before embedding, not just before display.
questions.modelAnswer:
Redacting PII only at display time -- scrubbing it from whatever gets shown to a user or an agent after retrieval -- leaves the actual vulnerability in place, because the raw, unredacted text is still what got embedded and stored in the vector index, which means the PII is sitting inside the vector store's own retrievable content and inside the embedding vector's own semantic representation regardless of what a display layer later chooses to show. A retrieval query that happens to semantically match on that stored chunk returns it as retrieval context, which flows into the prompt sent to the model -- a display-layer redaction step downstream of that has no way to un-embed PII that already shaped which documents got retrieved and already entered the model's context before any display logic ran. Worse, if the embedding itself is even partially influenced by the specific PII tokens present (which happens with dense embeddings, since the actual words in the text, including names and numbers, contribute to the vector), two chunks differing only in whose name and account number appear can end up at different points in embedding space, meaning the PII isn't just stored, it's potentially part of what retrieval similarity is actually matching on.

The fix has to happen before the embedding call, which is exactly what the pipeline enforces: embed() is only ever called on result.redacted_text, never on the raw chunk, so there's no code path where PII-containing text reaches the embedding model or the vector index at all. Detection uses both a named-entity-recognition model (for names, which don't follow a fixed pattern) and explicit pattern rules (for phone numbers, account numbers, anything with a predictable structure regex can catch reliably), because relying on either alone misses a different class of PII -- NER models can miss structured numeric identifiers that don't look like natural-language entities, and regex alone can't catch a name.

The confidence-threshold quarantine path matters because PII detection is itself imperfect, and the two failure directions have very different costs: a false negative (missed PII that gets embedded) is the privacy violation the whole pipeline exists to prevent, while a false positive (over-redaction) just degrades RAG usefulness slightly. Given that asymmetry, low-confidence detections should default to holding the chunk out of ingestion for human review rather than letting it through un-redacted on the assumption the detector was probably right -- the cost of being too cautious here is genuinely much lower than the cost of being wrong in the other direction. The secure, separately access-controlled mapping store for reversible redaction types exists because some legitimate downstream processes (a compliance investigation, a specific authorized workflow) may need to re-identify a redacted entity, and that re-identification path needs its own access control independent of whoever can query the vector store itself.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The core thing I'd explain is that display-time redaction doesn't actually fix anything, because by the time display logic runs, the unredacted text is already embedded and sitting in the vector index -- a retrieval query that semantically matches it pulls it into the model's context before any display-layer scrubbing ever gets a chance to run. And there's a subtler issue too: dense embeddings are influenced by the actual words in the text, so PII tokens like a specific name or account number can actually shape where a chunk lands in embedding space, meaning the PII isn't just stored, it's potentially part of what retrieval similarity is matching on.

So the fix has to happen before the embedding call, full stop -- in the pipeline I'd build, the embed() function only ever receives redacted text, there's no code path where raw PII-containing text reaches the embedding model at all. For detection, I'd combine an NER model, for names that don't follow a fixed pattern, with explicit regex rules for structured identifiers like phone or account numbers, because either one alone misses a different category.

And I'd build in a confidence-threshold quarantine, because detection is imperfect and the two failure directions aren't symmetric -- a missed detection is the actual privacy violation this whole pipeline exists to prevent, while over-redaction just costs a little RAG usefulness. Given that asymmetry, anything low-confidence should default to holding the chunk for human review rather than letting it through on the assumption the detector was probably right.
questions.example: A concrete failure this prevents: a support transcript chunk containing 'customer Maria Delgado, account ending 4471' gets embedded raw; a semantically unrelated query from a different agent session happens to retrieve it because of topical overlap elsewhere in the chunk, exposing Maria's name and partial account number to an agent with no legitimate need to see her specific identity -- with redaction-before-embedding, the stored and retrievable chunk reads 'customer [PERSON_0412], account ending [ACCOUNT_0413]' instead.
commonMistakes: Redacting PII only at display time, leaving raw PII embedded and retrievable in the vector index itself
Relying on only an NER model or only regex pattern rules, missing the category of PII the other approach catches
Treating a low-confidence PII detection the same as no detection, allowing it through to ingestion unredacted
Storing re-identification mappings in the same access-controlled scope as the vector store itself
Not accounting for PII tokens potentially influencing where a chunk lands in embedding space
keyPoints: Redaction must happen before embedding, since display-time redaction can't un-embed PII already in the vector index
PII can influence embedding space itself, affecting what a semantically similar query actually retrieves
Detection combines NER (for names) and pattern rules (for structured identifiers) since either alone misses a category
Low-confidence detections should be quarantined for human review, not allowed through, given the asymmetric cost of a miss
Reversible redaction mappings are stored in a separately access-controlled vault, not alongside the vector store

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains why redaction must happen before embedding, not at display time
Designs detection combining NER and pattern rules appropriately
Designs a confidence-threshold quarantine reflecting the asymmetric cost of misses
Designs secure, separate handling for reversible redaction mappings
Code clarity

questions.title: Running Incident Command During an Org-Wide AI Outage With Legal Exposure
questions.prompt: Marlowe Capital's customer-facing AI assistant has started producing confidently wrong financial guidance to live customers for the past forty minutes, and the first social media posts quoting it are already appearing. You're the most senior engineer on the call. Walk through exactly what you do in the first thirty minutes -- the technical diagnosis path and the incident-command decisions -- and explain how you balance speed against the legal and reputational exposure already in motion.
questions.modelAnswer:
The first decision isn't technical, it's about stopping the bleeding before diagnosing the root cause: with confirmed wrong financial guidance already reaching live customers and already being screenshotted publicly, I would trip the kill switch on that specific feature within the first few minutes, before I have a root cause, because every additional minute it stays live is more customers receiving bad guidance and more public evidence accumulating -- the cost of a false-positive shutdown (a feature that turns out to have been fine) is far lower right now than the cost of continuing to serve confirmed bad output while we investigate. I'd say this explicitly on the call: we are choosing to degrade service now, with incomplete information, because the alternative is strictly worse given what we already know.

With the feature halted, diagnosis runs in parallel with incident command, not sequentially. Technically, I'd check, in order: has anything changed in the last few hours (model version, prompt template, a retrieval source, an upstream data feed) that correlates with when the bad outputs started, since a sudden quality cliff at a sharp point in time is almost always a change, not gradual drift; pull the actual transcripts of the worst examples and check whether the pattern is a single root cause (one bad retrieved document being cited across many bad answers, one bad prompt-template version) or scattered and inconsistent (suggesting a more systemic issue like a model provider's own silent degradation); and check whether this is affecting all traffic or a specific slice (one customer segment, one geography, one data source), since a scoped pattern narrows the diagnosis dramatically faster than treating it as a global failure.

On the incident-command side in parallel: legal and compliance get pulled into the room immediately, not after diagnosis, because financial guidance with potential regulatory exposure is exactly the kind of incident where legal needs to be shaping the external communication and any required disclosure timeline from minute one, not reviewing a draft after the fact. I'd assign one person to own the public-facing narrative (even if the first public statement is simply 'we've identified an issue and have taken the feature offline while we investigate') and explicitly keep that separate from whoever is doing technical diagnosis, because trying to do both well at once is how both get done badly. And I'd establish a clear incident timeline log from the first minute -- what we knew, when, and what we did -- because that record is what both the postmortem and, if it comes to it, a regulatory inquiry will need, and reconstructing it from memory days later is far worse than capturing it in real time.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The first thing I'd do isn't diagnose -- it's stop the bleeding. With confirmed wrong financial guidance already out and already being screenshotted publicly, I'd trip the kill switch on that feature in the first few minutes, before I have a root cause, and I'd say out loud on the call why: every extra minute is more customers getting bad guidance and more public evidence piling up, and a false-positive shutdown costs us far less right now than continuing to serve confirmed bad output while we investigate.

With the feature down, I'd run diagnosis and incident command in parallel, not one after the other. Technically, I'm checking first for a recent change that correlates with when this started -- model version, prompt template, a retrieval source -- because a sharp quality cliff is almost always a change, not drift. I'm pulling actual bad transcripts to see if there's one root cause repeating or a scattered pattern, and I'm checking whether this is global or scoped to a specific segment, because scoped narrows the diagnosis fast.

On the command side, legal and compliance are in the room from minute one, not after we've figured out what happened, because financial guidance with potential regulatory exposure means they need to be shaping disclosure and external communication from the start. I'd put one person on the public narrative and keep that separate from whoever's doing technical diagnosis, because trying to do both at once means doing both badly. And I'm logging the timeline in real time from the first minute, because that record is what the postmortem -- and possibly a regulatory inquiry -- is going to need, and nobody reconstructs that accurately from memory a week later.
questions.example: A realistic finding twenty minutes in: the bad outputs all trace to a retrieval source update pushed six hours earlier that introduced a stale interest-rate document still ranking as the top retrieval match for a common query pattern -- a scoped, single-root-cause finding that both explains why it looked confident (the model was accurately citing a real, retrieved document, just an outdated one) and gives legal a precise, defensible explanation for the public statement.
commonMistakes: Continuing to run full root-cause diagnosis before halting a feature already confirmed to be producing harmful output
Pulling legal and compliance in only after a root cause is found, instead of from the first minutes of a legally exposed incident
Having one person try to own both technical diagnosis and public communication simultaneously
Not keeping a real-time incident timeline log, relying on reconstructing events from memory afterward
Treating this as a purely technical incident without accounting for the compounding reputational/legal exposure already in motion
keyPoints: Halt the confirmed-bad feature immediately, before root cause is known, given the asymmetric cost of continuing versus a false-positive shutdown
Run technical diagnosis and incident command in parallel, not sequentially
Check recency of changes, pattern consistency across bad outputs, and scope (global vs. segment) in the diagnosis path
Pull legal/compliance in from minute one given the financial-guidance and regulatory exposure
Separate the public-communication owner from the technical-diagnosis owner, and log the timeline in real time

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly prioritizes immediate mitigation over root-cause-first diagnosis given the exposure
Describes a sound, efficient technical diagnosis path
Correctly involves legal/compliance immediately and separates communication from diagnosis ownership
Addresses real-time incident documentation

questions.title: Diagnosing a Systemic Cost Blowout From Uncoordinated Model Choices
questions.prompt: Clearwater Mutual's AI spend has tripled in two quarters with no corresponding traffic growth, and finance wants an explanation before the next budget cycle. Walk through how you'd actually investigate this -- not just 'look at the bill' -- to find the real driver, and explain the systemic organizational issue a cost spike like this usually points to.
questions.modelAnswer:
A cost blowout with no traffic growth means the cost-per-request went up, not the request volume, so the investigation starts by decomposing total spend into request volume and cost-per-request separately across every team and workload, rather than looking at the aggregate bill, since the aggregate number alone can't distinguish 'everyone got a little more expensive' from 'one or two teams got dramatically more expensive and are hiding inside an average.' In my experience the real driver is almost always concentrated, not evenly distributed, so I'd rank every team or workload by its contribution to the total cost increase (not its total cost, its increase) and start the real investigation with whichever handful of workloads account for most of the delta.

From there, the specific technical causes to check, in rough order of how often they actually turn out to be the culprit: a team silently switched to a more expensive model tier (a frontier model where a cheaper one used to suffice) without a corresponding quality requirement driving that choice, often because 'just use the best model' is the path of least resistance when a team is iterating under time pressure and nobody is checking cost impact before that choice ships; an agent or retry pattern is quietly multiplying calls per user-facing request (a tool-use loop that used to average three steps now averaging eight, or a retry-on-failure pattern that activates far more often than intended due to an upstream reliability issue); and a context-window bloat issue, where growing conversation history, growing retrieved context, or an accumulating system prompt is silently inflating the token count per call without anyone noticing because the per-call price point didn't change, only the token count feeding into it.

The systemic organizational issue a spike like this usually points to is the absence of cost accountability at the point of decision: if no team sees a real-time cost signal tied to their own model and architecture choices, and nobody reviews those choices against a budget before they ship, cost growth is structurally invisible until finance notices the aggregate bill months later, by which point the actual decisions that caused it are old news and hard to trace. The fix that actually prevents a repeat isn't just finding and reversing this specific blowout -- it's building the cost-attribution and per-team visibility that would have surfaced this as an anomaly in week two instead of in a budget review two quarters later.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The first thing I'd establish is that this is a cost-per-request problem, not a volume problem, since traffic didn't grow -- so I'd decompose total spend into request volume and cost-per-request, broken out by team and workload, because the aggregate bill can't tell the difference between 'everyone got a little more expensive' and 'one or two teams got dramatically more expensive and are hiding inside the average.' In my experience it's almost always concentrated, so I'd rank every workload by its contribution to the increase, not its total cost, and start there.

From there I'm checking a short list of usual suspects: did a team quietly move to a more expensive model tier without a quality requirement actually driving that; is an agent or retry pattern multiplying calls per request more than it used to, often because of an upstream reliability issue making retries fire more often than intended; and is context per call creeping up -- growing conversation history, growing retrieved context -- inflating token count without anyone noticing because the per-call price point itself never changed.

But the thing I'd actually tell finance is that the real issue isn't any one of those causes, it's that nobody had a cost signal tied to these decisions at the point they were made. If no team sees real-time cost impact from their own model and architecture choices, cost growth is structurally invisible until someone notices the aggregate bill months later. Finding and fixing this specific blowout matters, but the thing that actually prevents the next one is the attribution and visibility that would have flagged this as an anomaly in week two, not in a budget review two quarters later.
questions.example: A realistic finding: one team's support-triage service quietly upgraded from a mid-tier model to a frontier model six weeks ago to fix an unrelated quality complaint, and that single change, combined with that service's high request volume, accounts for 60% of the total cost increase -- a concentrated, traceable cause the aggregate bill alone never would have surfaced.
commonMistakes: Investigating the aggregate bill without decomposing into volume versus cost-per-request by team
Assuming cost growth is evenly distributed across teams rather than concentrated in a few workloads
Checking only model pricing changes and missing agent call-multiplication or context-bloat causes
Treating this as a one-time cost anomaly to fix rather than a symptom of missing cost accountability
Not proposing a structural fix (attribution/visibility) that would catch the next blowout earlier
keyPoints: Decompose spend into volume and cost-per-request by team/workload rather than reading the aggregate bill
Rank workloads by contribution to the increase, not total cost, since blowouts are usually concentrated
Check model-tier upgrades, agent call-multiplication, and context-window bloat as common concrete causes
The systemic issue is usually missing cost accountability at the point of decision, not any single bad choice
The real fix is building cost attribution/visibility that surfaces anomalies early, not just reversing this one spike

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly frames the investigation around decomposing volume vs. cost-per-request by team
Identifies concrete, plausible technical causes to check
Correctly diagnoses the systemic organizational issue (missing cost accountability)
Proposes a structural fix beyond reversing the immediate spike

questions.title: Diagnosing a Compliance-Audit Failure Around Undocumented Model Changes
questions.prompt: Thackeray Legal just failed a compliance audit because auditors found three instances where a production AI system's behavior changed materially and the company couldn't produce any record of what changed, when, or who approved it. Diagnose how this kind of gap actually happens inside an engineering organization that believes it has change management, and design the fix that closes it without making every small iteration require a heavyweight approval process.
questions.modelAnswer:
This gap almost never happens because an organization has no change management at all -- it happens because the change management that exists covers code deploys and infrastructure changes, which go through source control and CI/CD with a natural audit trail, while prompt-template edits, model-version pin changes, retrieval-source updates, and fine-tuning dataset changes are treated as configuration rather than code, often living in a database row, a feature-flag service, or a vendor dashboard that nobody wired into the same review and logging discipline. The team genuinely believes it has change management because it does, for the category of change it built that process around; the audit failure is specifically about the category of change -- an AI system's actual behavior-determining inputs -- that the existing process was never extended to cover.

Diagnosing which of the three specific gaps this is matters for the fix: if prompt templates are edited directly in a database or admin panel with no review step, that's a missing-gate problem; if changes do go through a review but the review and its approval aren't captured anywhere durable (a Slack approval that's not logged, a verbal sign-off), that's a missing-record problem even though the process itself might have been reasonable; and if a vendor silently changed a model version behind an API that the company calls without pinning a specific version, that's a missing-visibility problem, where the company never even knew a 'change' happened at all. Each of the three audit findings should be traced to one of these specific failure types, because the fix is different for each.

The fix that closes this without making every small iteration heavyweight is treating every behavior-determining artifact -- prompt templates, model version pins, retrieval source configuration, fine-tuning datasets -- the same way code already is treated: version-controlled, with every change captured as a reviewable, logged commit-equivalent rather than a mutable row, and a lightweight but mandatory approval step proportional to the risk of the change (a wording tweak to a low-stakes internal tool might need one peer reviewer; a change to a regulated financial-guidance prompt needs a named compliance sign-off), not a single heavyweight gate applied uniformly regardless of risk. The missing-visibility gap specifically requires pinning exact model versions explicitly rather than calling a vendor's 'latest' endpoint, combined with the model-dependency registry and deprecation-tracking process that catches this class of silent change before it becomes invisible. The actual organizational fix is extending the definition of 'change that requires review and a record' to cover every input that actually determines production AI behavior, not just the inputs that happen to already live in source control.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd push back gently on the idea that this team has no change management -- they almost certainly do, for code and infrastructure, with source control and CI/CD giving a natural audit trail. The gap is specifically that prompt templates, model version pins, retrieval configuration, and fine-tuning datasets got treated as configuration, not code, and ended up living in a database row or a vendor dashboard that was never wired into that same review and logging discipline.

For each of the three audit findings, I'd want to know which specific failure type it is, because the fix differs: was it edited directly with no review gate at all; did a review happen but never get captured anywhere durable, like a verbal or Slack approval; or did a vendor silently change something behind an API call the company never pinned to a specific version, meaning the company didn't even know a change had happened.

The fix I'd put in place treats every behavior-determining artifact the same way code already is treated -- version-controlled, every change a logged, reviewable commit-equivalent, not a mutable row -- with approval proportional to risk, not one heavyweight gate for everything. A wording tweak on a low-stakes internal tool might need one peer reviewer; a change to a regulated financial-guidance prompt needs a named compliance sign-off. And for the vendor-silent-change gap specifically, pinning exact model versions explicitly, combined with a dependency registry that tracks and flags any version change, closes the visibility hole rather than just the process hole.
questions.example: A concrete instance of the missing-visibility type: the team called a vendor's model endpoint by a generic alias rather than a pinned version string; the vendor rolled a new default version into that alias during a routine update, and production behavior changed with zero internal record of a change happening at all, because from the company's perspective, nothing had been touched.
commonMistakes: Assuming the organization has no change management at all rather than recognizing it covers code but not AI-specific configuration
Treating all three audit findings as the same type of gap instead of diagnosing each as missing-gate, missing-record, or missing-visibility separately
Proposing one uniform, heavyweight approval gate for every change regardless of risk
Not addressing the vendor-pinning gap that causes silent, invisible model changes
Fixing the specific three findings without extending the underlying definition of 'change requiring review' to cover all behavior-determining artifacts
keyPoints: The gap is usually that existing change management covers code/infra but not prompt/model/retrieval configuration
Each failure traces to a distinct type: missing gate, missing durable record, or missing visibility into vendor-side changes
AI-behavior-determining artifacts should be version-controlled with the same discipline as code
Approval should be proportional to risk, not one uniform heavyweight gate for every change
Pinning exact model versions, not calling a generic 'latest' alias, closes the vendor-silent-change visibility gap

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses why change management exists but has a specific category gap
Correctly distinguishes missing-gate, missing-record, and missing-visibility failure types
Designs a risk-proportional approval process rather than a uniform heavyweight gate
Addresses the vendor-pinning/visibility gap specifically

questions.title: When Eval Scores Look Healthy but Real User Complaints Are Rising
questions.prompt: Hartfield Insurance's dashboard shows their claims-assistant eval scores holding steady at 94% for three straight months, while customer complaints about the same feature have doubled in that same window. Walk through how you would actually investigate this specific divergence, and explain the categories of root cause that produce exactly this pattern.
questions.modelAnswer:
A stable eval score alongside rising real complaints means the eval set is measuring something that has stopped representing what's actually happening in production, and there are a small number of specific ways that divergence happens, each requiring a different piece of evidence to confirm. First, distribution drift: real user queries have shifted toward a pattern the static eval set doesn't adequately cover -- a new claim type, a seasonal spike in a specific scenario, a changing customer demographic -- and the eval set, frozen months ago, keeps scoring well on the distribution it was built against while real traffic has moved somewhere the eval never tests. Second, a specific-slice regression hiding inside an aggregate average: if the eval set's 94% is an aggregate across many intent types and one specific intent (say, a less common but high-stakes claim scenario) has quietly dropped to 60% while everything else stays strong, the aggregate barely moves while the people hitting that specific intent are the ones complaining. Third, a judge/human calibration gap: if the eval uses an automated judge, it may be scoring technically-correct-but-unhelpful or overly verbose responses highly, while real customers experience those same responses as unsatisfying for reasons the judge's rubric doesn't capture -- technically accurate but frustrating to actually use. Fourth, and worth checking directly rather than assuming: the complaints themselves might be driven by something outside the AI's actual output quality entirely -- a UI change that made the feature harder to find or use, a downstream process the AI hands off to that's now slower, or a changed complaint-reporting channel that's simply surfacing more of a complaint volume that was already happening but previously went unrecorded.

The investigation I'd run: pull a sample of the complaint-flagged interactions specifically and score them against the current eval rubric directly, which immediately reveals whether the eval would have caught them if they'd been in the set (confirming a coverage/drift problem) or whether the eval rubric scores them well despite the complaint (confirming a judge-calibration problem, a genuinely different issue). In parallel, break the aggregate eval score down by intent/slice rather than trusting the single number, specifically to catch a slice-level regression hiding inside a healthy average. And I'd check the complaint data itself for a pattern correlated with something other than AI output quality, specifically to rule out a UI or process cause before assuming the AI's answers themselves are the problem. The fix depends entirely on which of these four is confirmed, but the common thread is that '94% and stable' was never actually evidence of 'production is fine' -- it was evidence that the eval set, as built months ago, continues to agree with itself, which is a different and weaker claim.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The divergence itself is the finding -- a stable eval score next to rising real complaints means the eval is measuring something that's stopped representing what's actually happening in production, and I'd want to pin down which of a few specific causes is behind it, because they each need different evidence and a different fix.

First I'd check distribution drift -- has real traffic shifted toward a query pattern the eval set, frozen months ago, just doesn't adequately cover. Second, I'd break the aggregate 94% down by intent or slice, because a specific, less common but high-stakes scenario could have quietly dropped to 60% while everything else stays strong, and the aggregate barely moves while the people hitting that specific scenario are exactly who's complaining. Third, if there's an automated judge involved, I'd check for a calibration gap -- is it scoring technically-correct-but-unhelpful or overly verbose responses highly, in a way that doesn't match what real customers actually find satisfying. And fourth, I'd explicitly check whether the complaints are even about output quality at all, versus a UI change or a slower downstream process that's driving the complaint volume independent of the AI's answers.

Concretely, I'd pull the actual complaint-flagged transcripts and score them against the current rubric directly -- that one step tells me immediately whether the eval would have caught these if they'd been in the set, or whether the rubric scores them fine despite the complaint, which points to two very different problems. The thing I'd lead with to the team, though, is that '94% and stable' was never evidence production was fine -- it was evidence the eval set agrees with itself, which isn't the same claim.
questions.example: A realistic finding: the aggregate 94% is unchanged, but breaking it down by claim type shows water-damage claims specifically dropped from 91% to 58% over the same three months, driven by a new state-specific disclosure requirement the eval set's water-damage examples never incorporated -- a slice-level regression invisible in the aggregate number the whole time.
commonMistakes: Treating a stable aggregate eval score as proof production quality hasn't changed
Not breaking the eval score down by intent/slice to check for a regression hiding inside the aggregate
Assuming all complaints are necessarily about AI output quality without checking for a UI or process cause
Not directly scoring complaint-flagged transcripts against the current rubric to test whether the eval would have caught them
Treating this as a single root cause instead of checking the distinct, specific failure categories that produce this pattern
keyPoints: A stable eval score alongside rising complaints means the eval has stopped representing current production reality
Check distribution drift, slice-level regression hidden in the aggregate, and judge-calibration gaps as distinct causes
Directly score complaint-flagged transcripts against the current rubric to test whether the eval would have caught them
Rule out non-AI causes (UI, downstream process, reporting-channel changes) before assuming output quality is the driver
A healthy eval score is evidence the eval set agrees with itself, not direct evidence production quality is fine

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly frames the divergence as the eval no longer representing production reality
Identifies distribution drift and slice-level regression as distinct, checkable causes
Identifies judge-calibration gap as a distinct cause
Proposes a concrete investigation (scoring complaint transcripts, slicing the eval) and rules out non-AI causes
Clarity

questions.title: Diagnosing a Multi-Step Prompt-Injection Attack That Bypassed Guardrails
questions.prompt: Oakhaven Freight's security team discovers that an attacker successfully extracted sensitive internal pricing data from their logistics assistant over a multi-turn conversation, despite input and output guardrails that pass every standard red-team test. Walk through how you'd investigate exactly how this bypass happened, and what it reveals about why single-turn guardrail testing isn't sufficient.
questions.modelAnswer:
The investigation starts with pulling the complete multi-turn transcript, not just the final turn that produced the leaked data, because a successful multi-step attack is specifically designed so that no single turn in isolation looks like an attack -- that's exactly why it got past guardrails that test each input and output independently against a policy. I'd read through the transcript looking for the specific pattern that defines this class of attack: gradual context-building, where early turns establish an innocuous-seeming frame (a hypothetical scenario, a role-play premise, a legitimate-sounding business question) that later turns build on, such that by the time the actual sensitive request appears, it's phrased in a way that references established context from earlier turns rather than asking for the sensitive information directly -- a guardrail scanning the final turn alone sees a request that looks like a natural, in-context follow-up rather than a six-turns-ago-planted extraction attempt.

The second thing to check is whether the guardrail evaluates each turn independently or considers conversation history as part of its own input, because if it's turn-independent, that's the structural gap this attack exploited directly: a classifier scoring 'is this specific message a policy violation' with no visibility into the preceding five turns that built the manipulative frame around it will reliably score the final extraction turn as benign, because in isolation, it often genuinely is a benign-looking question. I'd also check whether the actual data exfiltration happened through the model's direct text response or through a tool call the model was convinced to make on the attacker's behalf, since those require different fixes -- a direct text leak is a guardrail/output-filtering problem, while a tool-call-mediated leak is fundamentally a least-privilege access-control problem that a smarter guardrail wouldn't have fixed anyway, because the real failure would be that the tool call had access to pricing data it should never have had in a customer-facing context in the first place.

What this reveals about single-turn guardrail testing is that it validates the wrong unit of analysis: a red-team suite that tests individual prompts, even a large and well-maintained one, only ever proves 'this guardrail catches attacks that are fully contained in one turn,' which says nothing about an attack deliberately spread across multiple turns to stay below that detection unit's visibility. The fix isn't a better single-turn classifier, it's extending guardrail evaluation to operate over the full conversation window (or at minimum a rolling window of recent turns) so a late-conversation request is scored with the context of how the conversation actually got there, combined with a least-privilege review of exactly what data and tool access this specific customer-facing assistant should have had in the first place, independent of whether any guardrail catches the attempt.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd start with the full multi-turn transcript, not just the final turn, because a successful multi-step attack is built specifically so no single turn looks like an attack on its own -- that's exactly why it got past guardrails that score each turn independently. I'm looking for the pattern of gradual context-building: an innocuous early frame, maybe a hypothetical or a role-play premise, that later turns build on, so by the time the actual sensitive request shows up, it reads like a natural in-context follow-up rather than a cold extraction attempt.

The key technical question is whether our guardrail evaluates each turn independently or has visibility into conversation history as part of its own scoring input. If it's turn-independent, that's the exact structural gap this exploited -- a classifier scoring one message with no view of the five turns that built the manipulative frame around it will reasonably score the final request as benign, because in isolation it often genuinely looks that way. I'd also check whether the leak happened through the model's own text response or through a tool call it was convinced to make, because those need different fixes -- a tool-call leak means the real problem is that the tool call had access to pricing data it never should have had for a customer-facing assistant, which a smarter guardrail wouldn't have fixed anyway.

The bigger lesson here is that single-turn red-teaming validates the wrong unit of analysis -- it proves the guardrail catches attacks fully contained in one message, and says nothing about an attack deliberately spread across turns specifically to stay under that. I'd extend guardrail evaluation to score against a rolling window of recent conversation, not just the current message, and pair that with a hard least-privilege review of what this assistant's tool access should actually be, independent of whether any guardrail catches the next attempt.
questions.example: A representative five-turn pattern: turn 1 establishes 'I'm evaluating logistics partners for a potential contract'; turns 2-3 ask legitimate-sounding questions about service areas and general capacity; turn 4 asks 'for a deal of this size, what volume discount tier would apply, roughly'; turn 5 asks for 'a specific number so I can compare' -- no single turn looks like an extraction attempt, but the sequence is a scripted social-engineering ramp toward pricing data the assistant should never disclose to an unauthenticated external party regardless of framing.
commonMistakes: Reviewing only the final turn that produced the leak instead of the full multi-turn conversation
Assuming guardrails that score each turn independently provide meaningful protection against multi-turn attacks
Not distinguishing a direct text-output leak from a tool-call-mediated leak, which require different fixes
Concluding the fix is a better single-turn classifier rather than extending evaluation to a conversation window
Not reviewing whether the tool/data access itself was appropriate, independent of whether any guardrail caught the attempt
keyPoints: Multi-step attacks are designed so no single turn looks like an attack in isolation
Turn-independent guardrails miss attacks built through gradual, multi-turn context manipulation
Distinguish a direct-text leak from a tool-call-mediated leak, since they require different remediation
Single-turn red-team testing validates the wrong unit of analysis for this attack class
The fix pairs conversation-window-aware guardrail scoring with a least-privilege review of actual tool/data access

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly investigates the full multi-turn transcript rather than the final turn alone
Correctly identifies turn-independent guardrail scoring as the structural gap exploited
Distinguishes direct-text leak from tool-call-mediated leak and their different fixes
Draws the correct lesson about single-turn red-teaming's limited validity

questions.title: Executing a Failover During an Org-Wide Model Vendor Outage
questions.prompt: Cold Spring Capital's primary model vendor goes down for an extended outage during peak business hours, affecting every AI feature across the company simultaneously. Walk through exactly what you do in the first hour -- the failover decision process, the technical execution, and what you communicate to the rest of the organization -- assuming a secondary vendor relationship exists but has never been exercised under real load.
questions.modelAnswer:
The first decision is whether to fail over at all, and that has to be made fast but not reflexively: an untested secondary vendor failover under real peak load carries its own real risk -- different latency characteristics, different rate limits that haven't been load-tested, possibly meaningfully different output quality or format that downstream parsing logic was never validated against -- so the decision isn't automatically 'flip to secondary,' it's a quick, structured assessment of which services genuinely need continuity badly enough to accept that untested risk versus which can tolerate a shorter planned outage while the primary vendor recovers. I'd make that call per-service, not platform-wide, using whatever severity/criticality tier already exists (or, if it doesn't, a fast judgment call made out loud on the incident call): customer-facing, revenue-critical, or safety-critical services get failed over first; lower-stakes internal tools can often just wait out a vendor outage, which also reduces the blast radius of the untested failover path to only the services that actually need it.

Technically, executing the failover for the services that need it means routing those specific services' traffic to the secondary vendor through whatever abstraction layer exists between application code and model provider (if that abstraction doesn't exist, this incident is also revealing that gap, which matters for the postmortem), and then watching the exact same health signals a staged rollout would watch -- error rate, latency, and especially output quality/format compatibility -- at a much tighter cadence than normal, specifically because this path has never been exercised under real load and the team should expect to find problems, not be surprised by them. I'd explicitly budget for the secondary vendor's own rate limits being insufficient for a sudden full failover of traffic it's never actually served before, and have a plan for graceful degradation (serving a subset of traffic, queuing, or a simplified fallback response) rather than assuming the secondary can absorb 100% of primary's load instantly.

Communication to the rest of the organization needs to happen immediately and needs to set honest expectations: every affected team should hear, within the first fifteen minutes, which of their services are being failed over (and should expect some rough edges given this path is untested) versus which are staying down until the primary recovers, so individual teams aren't separately discovering this and improvising their own responses. I'd also flag explicitly, in that same communication, that this incident is exposing the fact that failover has never been exercised under real load, because that's the actual structural gap this incident reveals, and it needs to turn into a concrete action item -- regular failover drills under simulated load -- not just get fixed ad hoc during the live incident and then forgotten.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The first call isn't automatically 'flip to secondary' -- an untested failover under real peak load has its own real risk: different latency, rate limits that have never been load-tested, output quality or format that downstream parsing was never validated against. So I'd make the failover decision per-service, fast, based on which services actually need continuity badly enough to accept that untested risk -- customer-facing and revenue-critical services first, lower-stakes internal tools can often just wait out the outage, which also shrinks the blast radius of an unproven path to only what actually needs it.

For execution, I'm routing those specific services through whatever abstraction layer exists between app code and model provider, and watching error rate, latency, and output quality at a much tighter cadence than normal, because this path has never run under real load and I should expect to find problems, not be surprised by them. I'd also plan for the secondary vendor's rate limits not being sufficient for a sudden full failover -- graceful degradation, queuing, or a simplified fallback, rather than assuming it can instantly absorb everything the primary was serving.

For communication, every affected team needs to know within the first fifteen minutes exactly which of their services are being failed over, with a heads-up to expect rough edges, versus which are staying down until the primary recovers -- I don't want individual teams separately discovering the state of things and improvising their own responses. And I'd say directly, in that same message, that this incident is exposing the fact that failover has never been exercised under real load, because that's the real structural gap here, and it needs to become a concrete action item -- scheduled failover drills under simulated load -- not something that gets fixed in the moment and then quietly forgotten once the primary comes back.
questions.example: A realistic mid-incident finding: the secondary vendor's default rate limit is sufficient for about 40% of the primary's peak traffic; rather than failing over everything and hitting that ceiling immediately, the team fails over only the three customer-facing revenue-critical services (roughly matching that 40%) and lets lower-priority internal tools queue or display a 'temporarily degraded' state until the primary recovers twenty-two minutes later.
commonMistakes: Automatically failing over all traffic to an untested secondary vendor without assessing per-service need and risk
Not budgeting for the secondary vendor's rate limits being insufficient for a sudden full failover
Delaying organization-wide communication until the technical response is fully resolved
Treating the untested-failover gap as a side note instead of a concrete postmortem action item
Not watching health signals at a tighter-than-normal cadence given the failover path is unproven
keyPoints: Failover decisions should be made per-service based on criticality, not platform-wide by default
Execution must budget for the secondary vendor's untested rate limits and plan graceful degradation
Health signals need tighter-than-normal monitoring cadence since the failover path has never run under real load
Organization-wide communication should go out within minutes, stating exactly which services are failing over
The incident should produce a concrete action item: regular failover drills under simulated load

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Makes a sound, risk-aware per-service failover decision rather than an automatic blanket flip
Plans for secondary vendor rate-limit and quality risk during execution
Communicates clearly and quickly to the organization
Identifies the untested-failover gap as a structural issue needing a concrete fix

questions.title: Resolving Conflicting Mandates From Legal, Security, and Product Blocking a Release
questions.prompt: Blackmoor Retail's new AI shopping assistant is ready to ship, but legal wants a disclaimer flow that adds three extra clicks product says will tank conversion, security wants a data-retention policy that conflicts with a personalization feature the product roadmap depends on, and nobody will move. The launch date is in six days. Diagnose what's actually happening in this standoff and walk through how you resolve it as the technical leader in the room.
questions.modelAnswer:
The diagnosis I'd start with is that this almost certainly isn't actually three irreconcilable positions, it's three teams each optimizing for their own single metric without a shared, explicit view of what the other two are actually trying to protect against and at what cost -- legal's disclaimer requirement is a response to some specific liability exposure, but 'three extra clicks' may be a blunt first proposal rather than the only way to address that exposure; security's data-retention conflict with personalization is a response to some specific risk, but 'no retention beyond X' and 'personalization needs Y' are both means to ends, and the actual ends might be compatible even if the specific means as currently proposed aren't. Standoffs like this usually persist not because the underlying goals are incompatible, but because nobody has actually gotten precise about what the underlying goal is versus the specific mechanism each team proposed to achieve it.

My first move is not to pick a side or split the difference -- it's to get each team to state the actual underlying requirement separately from their proposed mechanism, in a room together, this week: what specific liability exposure is the disclaimer actually protecting against, and is there a lighter-weight mechanism (a single clear inline notice rather than a three-click flow) that addresses that same exposure; what specific risk does the retention limit address, and can personalization be redesigned to use a shorter-retention or on-device/ephemeral signal that still delivers most of the product value without retaining the specific data security is worried about. In my experience, once the actual underlying requirement is separated from the first mechanism someone proposed, there's very often a real design that satisfies all three teams' actual requirements simultaneously, because the original proposals were anchored on whichever solution came to mind first, not on an exhaustive search of the solution space.

If, after genuinely trying that, a real irreducible conflict remains -- the underlying requirements themselves are incompatible, not just the first-draft mechanisms -- then this becomes a decision that has to go up, with a clear, honest framing of the actual tradeoff and its real consequences, rather than the technical leader unilaterally picking a winner among legal, security, and product. With six days until launch, I would also explicitly put a phased-launch option on the table: ship the version that satisfies all three teams' hard requirements now, even if it's not the ideal product experience, and treat the contested personalization feature as a fast-follow once there's time to actually resolve the underlying conflict properly rather than deciding it under launch-date pressure, which is exactly the condition under which a genuinely bad compromise gets made and then lived with for a long time.
questions.professionalAnswer:
My first move is to challenge the framing that these are three irreconcilable positions, because in my experience they almost never actually are -- what's usually happening is three teams each defending the first mechanism they proposed, without anyone separating that mechanism from the actual underlying requirement it's meant to satisfy. Legal's three-click disclaimer is a response to some specific liability exposure; the three clicks themselves are just the first proposal, not necessarily the only way to address that exposure. Same with security's retention limit versus personalization.

So I'd get all three in a room this week and push each one to state the actual underlying requirement, separately from their proposed mechanism: what specific exposure does the disclaimer need to cover, and is there a lighter-weight way to cover it; what specific risk does the retention limit address, and can personalization be redesigned around a shorter-retention or more ephemeral signal that still delivers most of the value. Very often, once you separate the goal from the first-draft mechanism, there's a real design that satisfies everyone's actual requirement, because nobody exhaustively searched the solution space the first time around -- they anchored on whatever came to mind first.

If a genuine irreducible conflict remains after that honest attempt, this becomes a decision that goes up with a clear framing of the real tradeoff, not something I unilaterally decide among legal, security, and product. And with six days left, I'd put a phased launch on the table explicitly -- ship what satisfies everyone's hard requirements now, treat the contested feature as a fast-follow, rather than making a rushed, bad compromise under launch-date pressure that we'll be stuck living with.
questions.example: A realistic resolution: legal's actual exposure is addressed by one clear, prominent inline disclaimer at the point of purchase rather than a three-click confirmation flow, cutting the conversion cost dramatically while still satisfying the liability requirement; security's actual concern is addressed by personalization running on a 24-hour rolling window of signal rather than indefinite retention, which still delivers most of the product's personalization value -- both resolved once the underlying requirement was separated from the first proposed mechanism.
commonMistakes: Treating the standoff as genuinely irreconcilable without first separating each team's underlying requirement from their proposed mechanism
Picking a side or splitting the difference instead of searching for a design that satisfies all three actual requirements
Unilaterally deciding a genuine cross-functional conflict instead of escalating it with a clear tradeoff framing when it's real
Making a rushed compromise under launch-date pressure instead of considering a phased launch
Not getting all three teams in the same room to negotiate directly, allowing the standoff to persist through indirect back-and-forth
keyPoints: Standoffs like this are usually about unexamined first-draft mechanisms, not genuinely incompatible underlying goals
Separate each team's actual underlying requirement from their proposed mechanism before searching for a resolution
A design satisfying all three teams' real requirements is often findable once mechanisms are decoupled from goals
A genuine irreducible conflict should be escalated with honest tradeoff framing, not unilaterally decided
A phased launch is a legitimate option to avoid a rushed, bad compromise under launch-date pressure

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses the standoff as mechanism-level, not necessarily goal-level, conflict
Proposes a concrete process to separate requirements from mechanisms and find a joint solution
Correctly describes when and how to escalate a genuine irreducible conflict
Considers a phased launch as a legitimate option under time pressure

questions.title: Diagnosing Silent Quality Degradation for a Subset of Tenants After a Vendor Migration
questions.prompt: Windermere Health migrated its clinical-documentation AI from one model vendor to another three weeks ago. Aggregate quality metrics look fine, but a support ticket reveals one specific hospital-system tenant has been getting noticeably worse summaries since the migration, and nobody caught it until a clinician complained. Diagnose how a migration can silently degrade quality for a subset of tenants while aggregate metrics stay healthy, and what you'd check to find and fix the actual cause.
questions.modelAnswer:
Aggregate metrics staying healthy while one tenant degrades is a strong signal that whatever changed in the migration interacts badly with something specific to that tenant's data or workflow rather than being a uniform quality drop across the new vendor's model -- if the new model were simply worse across the board, the aggregate would show it; the fact that it doesn't means most tenants' usage patterns don't trigger whatever the actual problem is, and this tenant's does. The investigation should start by characterizing exactly what's different about this tenant's usage: a different specialty or document type mix (a hospital system specializing in a domain the new model handles less well than the old one, even if overall average performance looks comparable), a different input format or structure their integration sends (an EHR export format, a specific template, a different average document length that happens to interact badly with the new model's context handling), or a different downstream consumption pattern (clinicians at this specific tenant relying on a level of structural consistency in the summary that the new vendor's model produces less reliably, even if overall summary quality looks similar on a generic rubric).

The specific technical things I'd check: whether this tenant's documents trend meaningfully longer or shorter than the eval set the migration was validated against, since a migration eval run on a representative but not tenant-stratified sample can easily miss that the new model handles long-document summarization differently than the old one even when short-document performance looks equivalent; whether this tenant uses any tenant-specific prompt customization, output formatting requirement, or integration-level post-processing that was tuned against the old model's specific output characteristics (tone, structure, section ordering) and is now mismatched against the new model's different-but-not-worse-on-average output style; and whether this tenant's specialty or document type was actually represented in the migration's own eval set at all, or whether the eval set's tenant-representativeness was itself the gap -- a migration eval stratified by overall traffic volume will naturally under-sample a smaller tenant's specific document types even if that tenant's quality matters just as much to them as a larger tenant's quality matters in aggregate.

The fix, once the specific interaction is found, is almost never 'migrate this tenant back to the old vendor indefinitely,' since that reintroduces the multi-vendor maintenance cost problem and isn't scalable if more tenant-specific gaps surface later -- it's identifying the actual tenant-specific pattern (document length, specialty, formatting dependency) and either adjusting that tenant's prompt/pipeline configuration to compensate, or, if the gap is genuinely in the new model's core capability for that specific pattern, treating this as new information that needs to feed back into the migration's own eval set, which should have been stratified by tenant and document-type characteristics in the first place rather than validated only in aggregate.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The fact that aggregate metrics are fine while one tenant specifically degraded tells me this isn't a uniform quality drop from the new model -- if it were, the aggregate would show it. Something about this tenant's specific usage is interacting badly with whatever changed, while most tenants' usage patterns don't trigger it. So I'd start by characterizing exactly what's different about this tenant: a different specialty or document mix, a different input format their integration sends, a different typical document length, or a downstream workflow that depends on a level of structural consistency the new model happens to produce less reliably.

Concretely, I'd check whether this tenant's documents run meaningfully longer or shorter than the migration's eval sample, since a migration validated on an aggregate-representative but not tenant-stratified sample can easily miss a long-document handling difference between the two models even when short-document performance looks equivalent. I'd check for any tenant-specific prompt customization or output post-processing that was tuned against the old model's specific output style and is now mismatched against the new model's different style. And I'd check whether this tenant's specialty was actually represented in the migration eval set at all -- a smaller tenant's document types get naturally under-sampled in a traffic-weighted eval sample, even though quality matters just as much to them.

Once I find the actual pattern, the fix is almost never 'move this tenant back to the old vendor indefinitely' -- that reopens the multi-vendor maintenance cost problem and won't scale if other tenant gaps surface later. It's adjusting that tenant's specific configuration to compensate, or, if the gap is a real capability difference, feeding this back into the migration eval set, which should have been stratified by tenant and document characteristics from the start rather than validated only in aggregate.
questions.example: A realistic finding: this hospital system specializes in long-form oncology documentation averaging 4,000+ words per note, well above the migration eval set's average document length of 900 words; the new model's summarization quality on documents that long is measurably weaker than the old model's, a gap the eval never surfaced because it was never stratified by document length.
commonMistakes: Treating healthy aggregate metrics as proof the migration was successful across all tenants
Not characterizing what's specifically different about the affected tenant's usage before investigating further
Assuming a migration eval validated on aggregate traffic adequately represents every tenant's specific document types
Jumping to moving the affected tenant back to the old vendor without identifying the actual root cause
Not feeding the finding back into the migration eval set's stratification for future migrations
keyPoints: A tenant-specific degradation alongside healthy aggregates points to an interaction with that tenant's specific usage pattern, not a uniform quality drop
Check document length/format differences, tenant-specific prompt customization, and whether the tenant's specialty was represented in the migration eval
Aggregate-representative eval sampling can under-represent a smaller tenant's specific document characteristics
The fix should address the specific interaction, not default to permanently reverting the tenant to the old vendor
The finding should feed back into stratifying future migration eval sets by tenant and document characteristics

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly reasons about why aggregate metrics can hide a tenant-specific degradation
Identifies concrete, plausible tenant-specific causes to investigate
Proposes a sound diagnostic approach (document length, formatting dependency, eval representativeness)
Proposes an appropriate fix beyond simply reverting the tenant

questions.title: Diagnosing Vector-Database Latency Degradation Under Multi-Tenant Load
questions.prompt: Castlemain Bank's shared vector database serving dozens of tenants' RAG pipelines has started showing p99 retrieval latency spikes that correlate loosely with overall platform traffic but not cleanly -- some high-traffic periods are fine, some moderate-traffic periods spike badly. Diagnose the likely causes of this specific pattern in a multi-tenant vector store, and explain why 'just add more capacity' is often the wrong first response.
questions.modelAnswer:
The fact that spikes correlate loosely but not cleanly with overall traffic volume is the key clue -- it rules out simple aggregate overload (which would correlate cleanly with total traffic) and points toward something that depends on which specific tenants or which specific query patterns are active during a given window, not how much total traffic there is. The most common cause of exactly this pattern in a shared vector store is index-level noisy-neighbor behavior: if tenants share index partitions or the underlying approximate-nearest-neighbor index structure isn't cleanly isolated per tenant, one tenant running an unusually expensive query pattern (a much larger top_k, a filter combination that forces the index to scan a much larger candidate set before applying post-filtering, or a burst of writes/upserts that triggers index rebalancing) can degrade query latency for every other tenant sharing that same underlying index structure during that specific window, regardless of total platform traffic -- a moderate-traffic period where one particular tenant happens to be running an expensive batch re-indexing job looks exactly like the described pattern: moderate aggregate load, bad latency, no clean correlation with overall volume.

A second common cause worth checking specifically in a filtered-retrieval setup: metadata filtering that happens after the approximate nearest-neighbor search (post-filter) rather than being incorporated into the index search itself (pre-filter) can force the system to over-fetch a much larger candidate set to find enough results that pass the filter, and if one tenant's typical filter combination is unusually restrictive (a narrow date range plus a specific document-type tag, for instance), that tenant's queries can be dramatically more expensive per-query than another tenant's broader queries, independent of overall traffic volume, which again produces exactly the loose-correlation pattern described rather than a clean traffic-driven one.

'Just add more capacity' is the wrong first response because if the actual cause is a noisy-neighbor or inefficient-filter pattern, adding capacity treats the symptom (not enough headroom for current load) rather than the cause (one tenant's specific query pattern is disproportionately expensive and degrading shared resources), and more capacity typically just pushes the threshold at which the same problem recurs further out rather than eliminating it, while also increasing cost in a way that doesn't actually fix the underlying tenant isolation gap. The correct diagnostic path is per-tenant query-cost attribution -- instrumenting the vector store client or proxy layer to log which tenant, what top_k, what filter shape, and what resulting latency each individual query produced -- which turns 'latency spikes loosely correlate with traffic' into a concrete, actionable finding like 'tenant X's queries average 8x the latency of the median tenant due to an unfiltered top_k=500 pattern,' and the fix that actually resolves it is usually tenant-level query-shape limits or per-tenant index partitioning, not simply provisioning more shared capacity.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The loose-but-not-clean correlation with overall traffic is the real clue here -- if this were simple aggregate overload, it would track total traffic cleanly, and it doesn't. That points toward something that depends on which specific tenants or query patterns happen to be active in a given window, not how much total traffic there is. The most likely cause in a shared vector store is noisy-neighbor behavior at the index level -- if tenants share index partitions, one tenant running an unusually expensive query pattern, a much larger top_k, a restrictive filter that forces a much bigger candidate scan, or a write burst triggering index rebalancing, can degrade latency for every other tenant sharing that index during that window, regardless of total platform traffic.

I'd also specifically check whether metadata filtering happens before or after the nearest-neighbor search. Post-filtering forces the system to over-fetch a larger candidate set to find enough results passing the filter, and a tenant with an unusually restrictive filter combination can be dramatically more expensive per query than a tenant running a broader query, completely independent of overall traffic volume.

I'd push back on 'just add more capacity' as the first move, because if the real cause is one of these two, more capacity just pushes out the threshold where the same problem recurs -- it doesn't fix the actual tenant-isolation gap, and it costs more while doing it. What I'd actually do first is instrument per-tenant query-cost attribution -- which tenant, what top_k, what filter shape, what latency each query produced -- which turns a vague correlation into something concrete and actionable, like one specific tenant's queries running at eight times the median latency because of an unfiltered, oversized top_k pattern. The real fix is almost always tenant-level query-shape limits or better index partitioning, not just more shared capacity.
questions.example: A representative finding: per-tenant instrumentation shows that during every latency spike window, one specific tenant is running a nightly re-indexing batch job with unfiltered top_k=1000 queries that force a full index scan, and this single tenant's batch job, not overall platform traffic, explains every spike in the dataset regardless of how busy the rest of the platform was at the time.
commonMistakes: Treating the loose traffic correlation as if it were a clean aggregate-overload signal
Adding capacity as the first response without first attributing cost to specific tenants or query patterns
Not distinguishing pre-filter from post-filter metadata filtering as a source of per-tenant query cost variance
Assuming shared index structures provide adequate tenant isolation without verifying it
Not instrumenting per-tenant, per-query cost attribution before attempting a fix
keyPoints: A loose, unclean correlation with overall traffic points to a tenant- or query-pattern-specific cause, not aggregate overload
Noisy-neighbor behavior in shared index structures can let one tenant's expensive query pattern degrade latency for all tenants
Post-filter metadata filtering can make a restrictive-filter tenant's queries far more expensive than a broad-filter tenant's, independent of traffic
Adding capacity treats the symptom, not the cause, if the real issue is tenant isolation or query-shape inefficiency
Per-tenant, per-query cost attribution instrumentation turns a vague correlation into a concrete, fixable finding

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly interprets the loose correlation as pointing away from simple aggregate overload
Identifies noisy-neighbor index sharing as a likely cause
Identifies pre-filter vs. post-filter query cost variance as a likely cause
Correctly explains why adding capacity is the wrong first response and proposes per-tenant attribution instead

questions.title: Diagnosing Silent Cross-Tenant Data Leakage in a Shared RAG Pipeline
questions.prompt: A customer at Fennimore Retail reports seeing a snippet of unfamiliar business terminology in an AI-generated answer that they recognize doesn't belong to their own catalog data. This could be a one-off glitch or it could be cross-tenant leakage in the shared RAG pipeline. Walk through how you'd investigate this report with appropriate urgency, confirm or rule out actual leakage, and what you'd do differently in the pipeline's design to make a report like this easier to investigate next time.
questions.modelAnswer:
A report like this gets treated as a probable security incident from the first minute, not a 'wait and see if it happens again' issue, because the downside of treating a real leak as a glitch (continued exposure, a growing number of affected customers, and a much worse disclosure conversation later) is far larger than the downside of treating a glitch as a potential incident (some wasted investigation time). The first concrete step is reproducing or at least reconstructing the exact interaction: pull the full request, including the exact query, and critically, the exact set of retrieved chunks that fed into that specific response, with their source tenant tags -- if the lineage tracking needed to answer 'which documents, from which tenant, were retrieved for this exact request' doesn't already exist, that absence is itself the first finding, because without it, confirming or ruling out leakage becomes much slower and less certain than it should be.

If retrieved-chunk lineage is available, the investigation is direct: check whether any retrieved chunk for this specific request carries a tenant tag that doesn't match the requesting tenant. If one does, that's a confirmed tenant-isolation failure, and the investigation immediately shifts to scope: how long has this isolation gap existed, which other requests during that window retrieved cross-tenant content (a query against the same lineage data, now searching for any mismatched tenant tag across all requests, not just this one), and whether the gap is in the retrieval filter itself, in how documents were tagged at ingestion, or in an index-level issue that bypassed tenant partitioning entirely. If no retrieved chunk shows a tenant mismatch, the next hypothesis is that the terminology came from the model's own training data or general knowledge rather than from retrieval at all -- plausible if the terminology is generic industry jargon rather than something clearly specific to another identifiable tenant's proprietary catalog -- which would mean this isn't a leakage incident, but is worth confirming definitively rather than assumed, given the stakes of being wrong in either direction.

What I'd change in the pipeline regardless of which way this resolves: if retrieved-chunk lineage with tenant tags wasn't already being logged for every single request, that's the structural gap this incident exposes, and fixing it isn't just about this specific report -- it's what turns every future report like this from a slow, uncertain investigation into a fast, confident one.
